story-4de18bbd49569655af2715be.content: Japan Weighs US Defense AI for Military Command as Sovereignty Debate Grows Japan's Ministry of Defense is evaluating American military software to overhaul the command-and-control architecture of the Self-Defense Forces (SDF). The platforms under consideration include Palantir Technologies' Maven Smart System and Anduril Industries' Lattice, according to reporting from Nikkei Asia and the Asahi Shimbun. The drive toward these platforms stems from a stark operational reality: processing speed. While the US military uses systems like Maven to aggregate terabytes of satellite, radar, and sensor telemetry in real time, the SDF operates with virtually no AI inside its core command structure. Defense planners in Tokyo worry this processing gap creates a dangerous operational bottleneck during joint allied operations in East Asia. The Target-Selection Engine Under current proposals, Tokyo envisions deploying distinct software platforms for specific operational tasks, including counterattacks, missile defense, and unmanned drone networks. Rather than functioning as fully autonomous combat platforms, systems like Maven and Lattice operate as sensor-fusion layers. They pull raw data across surveillance assets, classify potential targets, and present optimized engagement options to military personnel. Under standard US and Japanese defense doctrines, target selection and firing authorization remain strictly subject to human command oversight. The Sovereign Data Dilemma Despite the push for modernization, the proposal has touched off intense debate inside Japanese government and defense circles. Plugging foreign software into national command structures requires feeding classified Japanese military intelligence through code owned and maintained by private US defense contractors. Even if physical data centers are constructed on Japanese soil, the SDF would remain dependent on overseas vendors for software updates, system patches, and ongoing operational capabilities. A Temporary Bridge to Domestic AI To balance speed with national security, Japanese officials are weighing a phased rollout. The government plans to revise key national security strategy documents to formalize military AI adoption, with several lawmakers advocating for a hybrid approach. Under this model, US software would serve as an interim solution to rapidly raise SDF capabilities while domestic tech firms develop a homegrown Japanese defense AI platform for the long term. Global Scrutiny and Geopolitical Friction The evaluation comes amidst broader international pushback against private defense tech vendors. European nations, including Spain, France, and Germany, have restricted or phased out state contracts with foreign data analytics platforms over data sovereignty and legal concerns. As Japan prepares to update its defense documents, Tokyo faces a tight balancing act between operational readiness with US allies and long-term technological independence. story-4e63823252fee2a6b34eccb8.content: Russia and North Korea are nearing completion of their first dedicated road bridge across the Tumen River, marking a major expansion of transport links between the two countries. The approximately 1-kilometre crossing connects Russia’s Khasan area with Tumangang in North Korea and will supplement the existing railway bridge. Once operational, it is expected to support up to 300 vehicles per day. The bridge structure and most facilities on the North Korean side appear largely complete. However, satellite imagery indicates that Russia’s much larger customs complex and connecting infrastructure remain unfinished, delaying the opening beyond the original June target. Moscow and Pyongyang officially describe the project as a route for expanding trade, tourism and passenger traffic. Analysts warn it could also strengthen military logistics, allowing personnel, equipment and concealed cargo to move between the two countries by road. Approximate coordinates: 42.4120°N, 130.6458°E

story-50aedc027bf42b5e795e21c9.content: AI failures are scattered across headlines. This repo puts the evidence in one place. Awful AI is a curated GitHub list tracking concerning uses and misuses of AI for builders, researchers, and anyone studying AI’s social impact. It helps you examine recurring risks by organizing cases into categories and pairing each entry with a summary, details, and source references. Key features: • Eight misuse categories – browse discrimination, disinformation and fakes, surveillance, data crimes, social credit, scams, climate impact, and autonomous weapons • Source-backed entries – each table provides an application, short summary, expanded context, and references • Counter-efforts included – explore privacy-preserving research, fair ML, adversarial ML, and projects designed to challenge harmful uses • Annual case record – review Awful AI Award entries covering controversial research and events from 2019 through 2024 • Citable collection – the README includes a Zenodo DOI for referencing the list in other work It’s open-source (CC0 1.0). story-55149370a1a5f04a8d920d47.content: ... but it is what's happening? Don't you think? The particular part of this segment I always liked is that it answers a question I always asked. Which is, why is it that no matter how much people may claim to hate Facebook or google or X or whatever. No matter how much people may claim to hate authority and centralized power. No matter how many times people have tried to create some exodus to elsewhere over fears of overreaching authority, surveillance or other. It never seems to happen. Actually the opposite tends to be the case. Because at some level people are attracted to what they sense as more powerful than them. Even if malicious in theory, or proven by evidence, they are still drawn to it. Because they'd rather have the sense that they are in association with something more powerful than not be. The absence of the sense of such a power creates anxiety. They need to feel like they know where the most powerful thing is and their relation to it. This is why it's impossible to ever create an exodus from such social platforms by presenting them as more free, more private, less surveilling, less "powerful" in some way. It's only a niche subset of crazy weirdos that desire true freedom and agency. People in general pool around what they sense is more powerful. If you ever actually wanted to pull off an exodus to some new social platform. You wouldn't want to sell it on privacy or freedom or anything which makes them feel like it has less power. You'd want to present something which exerts even more power, surveils even more, has the ability to effect even more. But not so much it scares people away like some scary beast. It has to sit there calmly, with passively demonstrably greater power in some way. For instance. If you had some social VR platform which exhaustively tracked everyones biometrics and then fed that into some matchmaking system to pair people with partners, and new friends, that actually worked. And it could direct human social pairing better than anything else. Masses would willingly just give up any and all biometric data. If even if it didn't work very well. Just the hope and sense of such a power would evoke that response. So I think it's just something you have to accept. It's what human nature wants. Everyone is going to end up consolidated around some massive data center with some super intelligent AI system that will interject itself into every little faucet of everyday human social life. Probably end up with the masses of people around each super AI being driven to war with one another amongst swarms of military AI drones. People may bemoan horrors and complain endlessly about so many things but never will any critical mass fully disband. Even if some super AI directed it's drone swarms to commit the grandest atrocities against humanity during wartime, after all the dust settles, that will just make people even more drawn to that particular super AI. Just look at what happened to the USA after WW2. Turned into the hottest place to be in the world.

story-5618d062693d03f6bbbac5a9.content: GLOBAL #SECURITY AND #INTELLIGENCE #NEWS REVIEW - AI REPORT: IRAN'S MILITARY STRATEGY Iran's military is on the defensive; deep underground - Search Iran's Underground Military Strategy https://t.co/46wd3zbKcr While it is true that Iran relies heavily on extensive subterranean networks to protect its military assets, characterizing its overall posture as purely "on the defensive" misses the strategic intent behind these facilities. Iran's use of deep underground bases is a calculated asymmetric strategy designed to ensure the survival of its offensive capabilities against adversaries with superior air power. Here is a breakdown of how Iran is currently utilizing its underground infrastructure and adapting its military posture: The Strategic Purpose of Underground Networks Iran's military doctrine emphasizes survivability through concealment and dispersal. By moving critical infrastructure deep underground, Tehran aims to neutralize the threat of precision strikes and bunker-busting munitions. Asset Protection: Iran houses a vast array of its military hardware in mountain tunnels, including air defense systems, ballistic missile stockpiles, drone production factories, and even naval speedboats. Operational Continuity: These fortified facilities are not just storage bunkers; they are active operational hubs. The goal is to maintain the ability to launch retaliatory or offensive strikes even while under sustained bombardment. Retaining Offensive Capabilities Despite sustaining damage in recent conflicts, intelligence assessments indicate that Iran's military retains significant striking power. Rapid Reconstitution: Recent reports from mid-to-late 2026 suggest that Iran has been rapidly rebuilding its capabilities, reopening underground missile facilities, and resuming weapons production at a pace that has alarmed Israeli and U.S. planners. Maintained Stockpiles: Classified U.S. intelligence assessments from earlier in 2026 contradicted public claims of a shattered Iranian military, noting that Tehran had retained roughly 70% of its prewar missile stockpile and mobile launchers, and had operational access to the vast majority of its underground storage. Tactical Adaptation Rather than simply hiding, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is actively adapting its battlefield tactics. Dispersed Air Defense: Iran claims to have replaced its conventional air-defense structure with a more flexible, dispersed network that improves intelligence-sharing and allows systems to function under attack. Recently, a mysterious new "Pantsir-like" air defense system was spotted inside an underground base, suggesting ongoing modernization. Asymmetric Warfare: The IRGC continues to refine its tactics to challenge U.S. and allied air defenses. This includes combining cheaper drones with maneuverable missiles in "swarm" tactics designed to overwhelm advanced defense shields and force adversaries to deplete expensive interceptor stockpiles. In essence, Iran's retreat underground is not a sign of capitulation, but a deliberate effort to preserve its "Hidden War" tempo. By protecting its missile and drone assets within fortified mountains, Tehran maintains a persistent, asymmetric threat projection across the region. - Iran's military is on the defensive; deep underground - Search AI Overview: Iran has increasingly shifted its military strategy toward deep-underground and mountain-fortified infrastructure ("missile cities") to protect its core missile, drone, and naval assets from heavy U.S. and Israeli airstrikes. While intensive Allied bombing campaigns have targeted tunnel exits and launch sites, intelligence assessments indicate that much of Iran's fortified subterranean network remains operational and preserves a substantial portion of its strategic arsenal.

story-57a97fd4854215ca92a051f4.content: Trump’s Art of the Deal: Total US casualties exceeded 770 since the conflict with Iran began on February 28, 2026. Pentagon data lists 18 service members killed and 757 wounded (primarily from traumatic brain injuries), following updates to the Defense Casualty Analysis System under the "Epic Fury" and "Overseas Operations" categories. Independent assessments from BBC Verify and The Washington Post indicate that the scale of infrastructure destruction is significantly wider than what the Pentagon originally acknowledged. Total Sites Hit: Analysts have identified confirmed damage at 20 to 28 specific U.S. installations. Structures Destroyed/Damaged: At least 228 individual structures or key pieces of tactical equipment have been struck region-wide. This includes aircraft hangars, barracks, fuel depots, radomes, and command headquarters. Severe Operational Closures: The U.S. 5th Fleet Naval Base in Bahrain (Naval Support Activity Bahrain) was hit so severely that it was reported as rendered inoperable. Beyond physical infrastructure, the strikes have exacted a staggering toll on U.S. military assets stationed at these bases, totaling between $13 billion and $29 billion in repair and replacement costs. Aircraft Losses: At least 42 U.S. military aircraft have been destroyed or severely damaged on the flight lines, including multi-million-dollar Boeing E-3 Sentry platforms and KC-135 refueling tankers. Drone Losses: At least 11 MQ-9 Reaper drones have been downed or destroyed. Air Defenses: Over a dozen critical radar systems, satellite antennas, and missile defense batteries (Patriot and THAAD) were successfully targeted and compromised.

story-598b4866cdb9ee743318a0d1.content: https://t.co/dM5UjuTftU NYT: Without Anthropic’s powerful Mythos model, it would be far more difficult for the National Security Agency to find and patch vulnerabilities in the Pentagon’s own systems, senior N.S.A. officials argued. And it turned out that, despite the original Anthropic ban, the N.S.A. was still allowed to use its products. Critical tests were underway using Mythos to gauge its potential to hack into highly protected foreign networks, current and former officials said. Shutting down the use of Mythos, an A.I. model whose potential for conducting offensive cyberoperations is already shifting the digital arms race into overdrive, would have amounted to “unilateral disarmament,” according to one recently departed senior U.S. official. From the Department of Defense to the C.I.A. and N.S.A., billions have already been spent on using artificial intelligence to develop weapons that could work with less human control, or to test vulnerable military networks and even nuclear codes to make sure they cannot be cracked by adversarial A.I. systems. Artificial intelligence is critical to the Golden Dome. But little of that work anticipated the powers of Mythos and its A.I. counterparts, or the prospect that China may be months away from its own formidable and less expensive versions. That could supercharge China’s ability to infiltrate American communications networks, water systems and power grids.

story-5a170897d02a9c09a7fead3e.content: CENTCOM announced a new bilateral task force with the UAE on July 28, "Talon Synapse," focused on accelerating military AI applications, set to formally launch in the coming weeks. The Abu Dhabi-based team will include roughly 20 American and Emirati personnel specializing in AI, data, and cybersecurity, focused on intelligence support, critical infrastructure protection, and monitoring the regional security environment. Adm. Brad Cooper, CENTCOM commander: "This will be a historic milestone as we work with one of our most capable regional partners to rapidly deliver evolving AI advancements to our warfighters." The concept originated last year in discussions between Cooper and UAE National Security Advisor Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, with CENTCOM meeting AI industry leaders and Emirati officials during a regional trip last month. This lands the same week as the SpaceX-Pentagon computing talks, the Anduril Arsenal-1 production milestone, and Ukraine's own AI-enabled interceptor systems, part of a broader pattern of the U.S. military formalizing AI partnerships across multiple fronts simultaneously, even as CENTCOM's own conventional stockpiles, interceptors specifically, remain the actual bottleneck constraining operations in the same theater right now.

story-5a5153a10387448299375eac.content: Recent wars aren’t about borders, resources, or ideology the way the headlines claim. They’re deliberate, high-intensity data-collection operations engineered to feed the next generation of military AI. Live combat is the only environment that produces the exact telemetry, multi-domain sensor fusion under jamming, real-time command decisions under extreme uncertainty, cascading logistics failures, and human-AI interaction edge cases that no simulation, video game, or peacetime exercise can fully replicate. Ukraine, the Middle East, the ongoing proxy fights — every drone swarm, every precision strike log, every battle-damage assessment, every degraded communications trace becomes classified training data locked inside the military-industrial complex. Public AI labs are starving for this distribution. The contractors and agencies that actually control the collection systems are not. What’s truly tragic — and deeply wrong — is the thought that if this is even partly the reason, then countless lives, homes, and futures are being spent as the price of better training data. The battlefield isn’t just a laboratory. It’s a human catastrophe being harvested for algorithms that will shape the wars that come after.

story-5be8d3fbe9c16251eff5d042.content: 🌐 صناعة الذكاء الاصطناعي السيادي 💥هل يمكن لكاميرا صغيرة أن تتحول إلى بوابة استخباراتية؟ 💥 وهل أصبحت سلسلة التوريد العالمية أخطر من ساحة المعركة نفسها؟ 💥 ماذا يحدث عندما تُرسل معدات يُفترض أنها تحمي القوات العسكرية بياناتها إلى الإنترنت؟ 💥 وهل يكفي شراء منظومة عسكرية من شركة موثوقة لضمان أمنها، أم أن الخطر قد يكون مختبئًا داخل أحد مكوناتها الإلكترونية؟ ✦ ─────────────────── ✦ 💥الصدمة أولاً في تطور أثار اهتمام الأوساط الأمنية والعسكرية، كشفت صحيفة التليغراف (The Telegraph) أن كاميرات صينية الصنع كانت مثبتة على طائرات مسيّرة وزوارق استطلاع بريطانية أرسلت بيانات اتصال إلى الإنترنت، ويشتبه أن تكون قد أرسلتها إلى الصين الأمر الذي أثار تساؤلات جدية حول أمن المعلومات في الأنظمة التي يُفترض استخدامها في مهام حساسة، من بينها عمليات المراقبة في مضيق هرمز (Strait of Hormuz). ورغم أن الكشف لا يعني بالضرورة حدوث تسريب لمعلومات عسكرية سرية، فإنه أعاد فتح ملف بالغ الحساسية يتعلق بأمن سلاسل التوريد (Supply Chain Security)، وإمكانية أن تتحول المكونات التجارية منخفضة التكلفة إلى مصدر مخاطر داخل الأنظمة الدفاعية. ✦ ─────────────────── ✦ 🏛️ لماذا أثارت القضية هذا القدر من القلق؟ تكمن المشكلة في أن أي جهاز إلكتروني حديث لم يعد مجرد قطعة من العتاد، بل أصبح حاسوبًا متصلًا بالشبكات ويحتوي على نظام تشغيل وبرمجيات وآليات تحديث واتصال. وعندما يظهر أن أحد هذه المكونات يحاول إنشاء اتصالات عبر الإنترنت داخل منظومة عسكرية، فإن الجهات الأمنية تعتبر ذلك حدثًا يستحق التحقيق، حتى لو لم يثبت وقوع اختراق فعلي. ففي البيئات العسكرية، يكفي وجود قناة اتصال غير متوقعة حتى تُعامل باعتبارها مخاطرة أمنية محتملة. ✦ ─────────────────── ✦ 🔍 ماذا حدث بحسب المعلومات المنشورة؟ • اكتُشف أن كاميرات صينية الصنع المثبتة على بعض الطائرات المسيّرة والزوارق غير المأهولة أجرت محاولات اتصال عبر الإنترنت. • هذه المنصات مخصصة لأعمال الاستطلاع والمراقبة البحرية. • من بين السيناريوهات التشغيلية المحتملة استخدامها لدعم العمليات في مضيق هرمز، أحد أكثر الممرات البحرية حساسية في العالم. • أثارت هذه الاتصالات تساؤلات حول ما إذا كانت ناتجة عن خصائص تقنية افتراضية، أو خدمات تحديث، أو إعدادات مصنعية، وهو ما يستوجب التحقيق الفني. • حتى الآن، لا يُعد مجرد الاتصال دليلًا على تسريب بيانات عسكرية أو وقوع عملية تجسس، لكن الخبراء ينظرون إليه باعتباره مؤشرًا يتطلب الفحص والتحليل. ✦ ─────────────────── ✦ 🌍 لماذا يُعد مضيق هرمز موقعًا شديد الحساسية؟ يمثل مضيق هرمز أحد أهم شرايين الطاقة والتجارة العالمية، وتعتمد عليه نسبة كبيرة من صادرات النفط والغاز المنقولة بحرًا. ولذلك فإن أي منظومة استطلاع تعمل في هذه المنطقة قد تتعامل مع معلومات تتعلق بحركة السفن، والأنشطة البحرية، وأنماط الانتشار العسكري، وهي بيانات تتمتع بقيمة استراتيجية مرتفعة. ✦ ─────────────────── ✦ 🧠 كيف يمكن أن يتحول جهاز بسيط إلى خطر أمني؟ تخيل أن لديك كاميرا مراقبة داخل منزلك. إذا كانت الكاميرا ترسل بيانات إلى خادم خارجي دون علمك، فحتى لو لم تُسرق صورك، فإن مجرد وجود قناة اتصال غير مصرح بها يمثل نقطة ضعف. الأمر نفسه ينطبق على المعدات العسكرية، ولكن مع فارق أن قيمة البيانات والنتائج المحتملة أعلى بكثير. لهذا أصبحت البرمجيات الثابتة (Firmware)، وأنظمة التشغيل المدمجة، وآليات التحديث، جزءًا أساسيًا من تقييم أي منظومة دفاعية. ✦ ─────────────────── ✦ ⚙️ لماذا أصبحت سلسلة التوريد ساحة صراع جديدة؟ تعتمد الصناعات الدفاعية اليوم على آلاف المكونات القادمة من شركات ودول مختلفة. وقد تحتوي المنصة العسكرية الواحدة على: • معالجات إلكترونية. • كاميرات رقمية. • رقائق اتصال. • وحدات تحديد مواقع. • أنظمة ذكاء اصطناعي. • برمجيات من موردين متعددين. ولهذا أصبح السؤال الأمني لا يقتصر على "من صنع الطائرة؟"، بل يمتد إلى "من صنع كل قطعة داخلها؟". ✦ ─────────────────── ✦ 🚨 أبرز المخاطر المحتملة • إنشاء اتصالات غير متوقعة مع الإنترنت. • زيادة مساحة الهجوم الإلكتروني (Attack Surface). • صعوبة التحقق من جميع البرمجيات المدمجة داخل المكونات التجارية. • احتمال وجود إعدادات افتراضية أو خدمات اتصال غير معطلة. • ارتفاع تكلفة فحص واعتماد المكونات قبل دمجها في الأنظمة العسكرية. ✦ ─────────────────── ✦ ✅ ماذا يمكن أن تتعلم منه المؤسسات والشركات؟ أصبحت المؤسسات الدفاعية والحكومية تتجه بصورة متزايدة إلى: • مراجعة جميع مكونات سلسلة التوريد. • إجراء اختبارات أمنية مستقلة قبل التشغيل. • عزل الأنظمة الحساسة عن الإنترنت متى أمكن. • تعطيل الخدمات والاتصالات غير الضرورية. • مراقبة حركة البيانات الصادرة باستمرار. • فرض معايير أكثر صرامة لاعتماد الموردين والمكونات الإلكترونية. ✦ ─────────────────── ✦ 🌐 البعد الجيوتقني تعكس هذه القضية تحول المنافسة الدولية من التركيز على الأسلحة التقليدية إلى التركيز على التكنولوجيا وسلاسل التوريد. فاليوم قد تصبح الكاميرا، أو الشريحة الإلكترونية، أو البرنامج الثابت، جزءًا من معادلة الأمن القومي، تمامًا كما هي السفن والطائرات والرادارات. ولهذا تتجه دول عديدة إلى إعادة تقييم اعتمادها على المكونات الأجنبية في القطاعات الحساسة، مع تعزيز التصنيع المحلي، وتنويع الموردين، وتشديد متطلبات الأمن السيبراني. ✦ ─────────────────── ✦ 📌 الدرس المستفاد من الدروس المستفادة لا تؤكد المعلومات المنشورة وقوع عملية تجسس أو تسريب بيانات عسكرية، لكنها تكشف حقيقة أكثر أهمية: أن الأمن العسكري في العصر الرقمي لم يعد يعتمد فقط على قوة المنصات القتالية، بل على الثقة بكل مكون إلكتروني داخلها. لقد أصبحت سلسلة التوريد نفسها ساحة مواجهة استراتيجية، وأصبح فحص الكود والبرمجيات والاتصالات لا يقل أهمية عن اختبار المحركات والأسلحة. وفي عالم تتزايد فيه الأنظمة المتصلة، قد تبدأ أخطر الثغرات من جهاز صغير يبدو للوهلة الأولى مجرد كاميرا. ✦ـــــــــــــــــــــــــــــــــــــــــ مع دخول story-5c301525261eddb6b825758a.content: OpenAI تقول: الخطر مو في قوة الذكاء الاصطناعي فقط… بل في مين يسيطر عليه OpenAI أطلقت مشروع بحثي جديد اسمه AI Futures، وفكرته تدرس كيف ممكن الذكاء الاصطناعي يغيّر شكل المجتمع والحكومات والقوة في المستقبل. اليوم الحكومات تعتمد بشكل كبير على الناس، سواء كموظفين، جنود، أو حتى من خلال الضرائب. لكن تخيل مستقبل فيه الذكاء الاصطناعي والروبوتات يقدرون يسوون جزء كبير من هذي المهام. مثلًا، ممكن أنظمة عسكرية ذاتية تنفذ مهام بدون الحاجة إلى أعداد كبيرة من الجنود، وممكن أنظمة ذكاء اصطناعي تدير أجزاء من العمل الحكومي بشكل آلي. وإذا صار جزء كبير من الثروة يطلع من مراكز البيانات والذكاء الاصطناعي بدل عمل البشر، هنا ممكن تتغير العلاقة بين الحكومة والمجتمع بشكل كبير. السؤال اللي تطرحه OpenAI هو: إذا صارت التقنية تعطي قوة هائلة لعدد قليل من الحكومات أو الشركات، كيف نحافظ على حقوق الناس وحريتهم وقدرتهم على اتخاذ القرار؟

story-5cbcc139bc7d3eccd7212623.content: This is where we are. Autonomy and governance are in tension, but they also depend on each other. Governance enables autonomy: rights (property, speech, bodily autonomy) only mean much when institutions enforce them. Without rules, "autonomy" for the less powerful collapses into domination by the more powerful. Governance limits autonomy: individual or unit-level freedom gets bounded for the sake of collective goods -- safety, coordination, preventing harm to others (state law, corporate hierarchy, AI oversight, public health mandates). Subsidiarity is the recurring design answer: push decisions down to the most local/autonomous level capable of handling them, with governance stepping in only when there's a failure, coordination problem, or risk of abuse. Legitimacy is the connecting thread: governance that oversteps autonomy without justification looks like overreach; autonomy with no accountability tends toward abuse. Most institutional design -- political, corporate, medical, or AI-related -- is really about calibrating how much autonomy to grant and what checks (consent, transparency, audits, appeals) apply to it.

story-63429a592b04ec04dd159362.content: Taiwanese authorities just detained an Nvidia sales manager and seized 50 high-end AI servers valued at $22 million bound for China. The raid on Nvidia’s Taipei office marks a dramatic escalation in closing supply chain backdoors that bypass trade restrictions designed to curb Beijing’s military AI ambitions. Investigators say the network forged customs declarations to ship servers through Japan before routing them into Chinese markets. The crackdown has already led to seven detentions, implicating key figures at server manufacturer Super Micro Computer and regional distributor Albatron Technology. Because Taiwan currently lacks a specific criminal law for unauthorized chip exports, prosecutors are charging suspects with forgery and breach of trust under the penal code. Nvidia maintains that diverted products receive no support or updates, but the case highlights how aggressively black-market brokers target global hardware networks. As illicit channels continue finding ways to feed Beijing's demand for advanced hardware, can Western trade controls ever fully secure the global supply chain?

story-63f25e09bce672908a9eeeff.content: The "WMD" is what AI was capable of doing. in 1999, NASA successfully tested its Remote Agent program, allowing the Deep Space 1 spacecraft to autonomously manage operations and correct faults in real time. This serves as an early operational milestone for intelligent, goal-directed software control. Autonomous flight algorithms rely on massive amounts of real-world telemetry data to learn how to operate under radio-frequency jamming, contested airspaces, and asymmetric electronic warfare. The Middle East provided an active operational environment and active war zones served as an accelerator and proving ground. Drones can easily fly by GPS or remote control in quiet U.S. test spaces. But in active combat zones, heavy electronic warfare and radio-frequency jamming instantly sever normal pilot signals. AI systems learn from seeing real threats, distinct weather, and chaotic battlefield telemetry. This provides developers with real-world operational data that simulated environments cannot accurately replicate. [But they aren't going to tell us this motive.] Cognitive weapons also absolutely require real-world human data and simulation to function effectively. Creating hyper-realistic, localized disinformation campaigns requires training AI on real-world cultural nuances, language patterns, and psychological vulnerabilities of specific populations. Algorithms simulate thousands of societal reaction scenarios to predict how public morale or military cohesion will fracture under specific cyber or physical pressures. Large language models and psychological AI tools are trained on information that people voluntarily put on the open internet—such as public social media posts, blogs, and public forums. Social media algorithms use basic cognitive principles to monitor what you look at, how long you linger on a post, and what makes you click. The goal of this commercial software keeping your attention to sell advertisements. However, because this technology maps human vulnerabilities so well, governments and militaries study these commercial patterns to understand how information spreads. Militaries map communication pathways to find bottleneck points in an enemy's command chain. By injecting precise information or static into those specific nodes, they slow down the enemy's ability to observe, orient, decide, and act. Knowing exactly how data moves allows a military to feed false indicators into an enemy's intelligence collection network. The AI or human analysts on the other side will then pass the engineered misinformation up the chain as verified truth. Algorithms identify existing social or political fractures within an adversary's population. Militaries use this map to seed hyper-targeted messaging that accelerates internal chaos, draining the adversary's domestic resources without firing a shot. By tracking the velocity and origin of an adversarial narrative, defense networks can deploy "pre-bunking" campaigns. This neutralizes enemy propaganda before it reaches a critical mass within the civilian population or military ranks. Real-time information tracking makes it nearly impossible for leaders to hold secret backchannel peace talks. Adversaries or domestic political factions can detect slight changes in flight patterns, official communication nodes, or digital chatter, leaking the talks early to sabotage a ceasefire before it can be finalized. To calculate the long-term success of a ceasefire, AI models use probabilistic game theory, machine learning classifiers, and system dynamics modeling. Peace deals rarely fail because a president changes their mind; they fail due to unpredictable, real-world friction. While these calculations are incredibly advanced, they suffer from a major flaw: AI cannot model unprecedented human choices. If a leader acts completely irrationally—defying their own economic, military, and survival interests due to a deeply personal or psychological whim—the AI's calculation completely breaks down. The model can only calculate what is statistically logical based on the data it has already seen. Donald Trump is notoriously difficult for standard AI models to predict because his decision-making relies heavily on intentional ambiguity and strategic noise. His communication style frequently involves floating a policy, threatening an action (such as tariffs), and then abruptly pausing or revoking it days later. AI models struggle to separate "noise" from actual policy shifts. Military and diplomatic models assume a leader will follow an established institutional pipeline. When a leader acts independently or changes standard frameworks entirely—such as his 2026 restructuring of national security AI directives—pre-built predictive assumptions break down. Furthermore, the underlying data powering these predictive models is heavily derived from the public digital footprints of everyday civilians. Militaries and defense analysts do not train global-stability models solely on top-secret data. Instead, they build "social simulations" that rely massively on the public data. When defense systems try to calculate if a peace negotiation will survive, they are not just trying to guess what a leader will do. They are using civilian data to map "stampede theory" and "informational cascades"—calculating how easily everyday citizens can be swayed by disinformation loops or economic stress, which ultimately forces the leader's hand. The scale of this has become so prominent that defense tech agencies are actively deploying AI tools to build comprehensive, detailed portraits of populations based on commercial and government database loopholes. Of note: civilian opinions get heavily and disproportionately weighted inside these models! AI stability and conflict models do not treat every internet user as an equal data point. Instead, they use data-science frameworks to find "nodes of high leverage." If a civilian is a "hub"—meaning thousands of other accounts read, share, or reply to them—their single opinion is heavily weighted. The AI knows that if a high-centrality influencer changes their opinion or posts an angry narrative, it will cause an "informational cascade" that can shift the mood of an entire city or region within hours. Because AI conflict models rely heavily on civilian digital footprints to predict public behavior and escalation, hostile actors can easily "game" the system to trick the algorithm. Intelligence agencies or adversarial groups like Pravda publish thousands of cheap, machine-generated articles, blog posts, and fake local forum entries containing specific tactical lies. Even if no real human ever reads those pages, the automated scrapers powering the military's open-source intelligence AI will ingest them. The AI slowly adopts those invented narratives as normalized baseline facts, filtering poisoned data straight up to top-level decision-makers. Because these AI models output incredibly precise-looking math—such as a "74% chance of ceasefire collapse"—human leaders tend to blindly trust the machine, especially when they are exhausted, frightened, or under immense time pressure. An adversary only needs to manipulate a tiny fraction of the underlying data points to alter that final percentage. If they can tweak the AI's calculation from a 40% threat level to an 85% threat level, they can use the human commander's own automation bias to force them into making a strategic error. Militaries are fully aware that their predictive software is highly fragile. To prevent getting tricked, they use specialized defensive layers: Specialized programs like DARPA's GARD (Guaranteeing AI Robustness against Deception) are designed to scan incoming data streams for abnormal mathematical patterns that indicate an enemy is trying to poison the dataset. Human-in-the-Loop (HITL): International defense frameworks strictly dictate that an algorithm can never make a final diplomatic or kinetic decision on its own. A human analyst must look at the raw evidence to determine if the AI's conclusion is being driven by real civilians or a coordinated digital deception campaign. Also of note: When intelligence agencies and military AI scan the internet, they do not care about your individual username or follower count. Instead, they look at how millions of small footprints fit together into a larger pattern. In modern military intelligence, every smartphone is treated as an unintentional battlefield sensor. If you have a small online footprint, you are actually highly valuable to predictive models because you represent the "silent majority". To know if an information campaign is working, an adversary's AI needs to know what normal, quiet civilians are talking about. Algorithms monitor small accounts to see if an extreme political narrative is jumping from loud influencers over to regular, everyday people. If quiet profiles suddenly start repeating a specific talking point or rumor, the AI flags it as a major policy risk, alerting leaders that public sentiment is shifting toward a tipping point. Once an AI perfectly understands the normal digital footprint of a quiet civilian, it can be used to generate hyper-realistic fake profiles ("puppet networks") that blend in perfectly with real society to manipulate public policy or spread confusion during a conflict. This data changes how leaders act in real time. For example, during geopolitical crises, defense analysts present leaders with automated sentiment charts compiled from millions of public X posts. If the data shows that a specific military strike will cause a massive, uncontrollable wave of panic or anti-government unity among regular citizens, politicians may cancel a military operation or alter their foreign policy entirely to avoid a catastrophic public backlash. Defense contractors and intelligence agencies use specialized software suites—such as Babel Street, Palantir Foundry, or Voyager Analytics—to passively vacuum up open-source data. These companies pay for direct, enterprise-level access to the "data firehose" of platforms like X and Reddit. They pull hundreds of thousands of posts per second. Advanced Natural Language Processing (NLP) models automatically read the text. It can translate local slang, filters out casual chat, and categorizes posts by theme (e.g., "infrastructure damage," "troop movement," or "civil unrest") based on the models architecture. When war broke out in Ukraine and during subsequent regional conflicts, civilian posts completely changed the timeline of battlefield intelligence. Even if a civilian explicitly deletes their location coordinates before posting a photo, modern AI can still find them. Also even when your device is completely offline, it continues to broadcast a low-power Bluetooth beacon signal. If an entirely random stranger walks past you with a connected smartphone, their phone secretly picks up your device's beacon and uploads your location to the cloud. When you turn off Wi-Fi and mobile data, your phone does not stop gathering data; it simply stops transmitting it. Your phone’s internal GPS chip keeps recording your exact coordinates, and internal motion sensors record your steps and movement patterns. "We're talking about software that's coming that if it stops working, it's going to kill people," Michael Saylor said in 2000. "And if it does work, it will save people." MicroStrategy would run this network and make billions in the process, which is Mike Saylor's job but not his goal. It's not why he was put on Earth. Saylor believes he was put here to change the world, to obliterate ignorance, to spread "intelligence everywhere." This was the vision. But billionaires needed the buy-in to make it happen. story-63fbd2f697abcd8f46b566c4.content: Alternate History: Operation Epic Fury — F-35s and HIMARS Only 28 February 2026 Operation Epic Fury begins with a restriction that shocks the Pentagon: the United States will attack Iran using only F-35 Lightning II fighters and HIMARS rocket artillery. No B-2 bombers. No Tomahawks. No F/A-18 strike packages. No large-scale drone attacks. The strategy is nicknamed Lightning and Thunder. The F-35 provides the eyes and the deep strike capability. HIMARS provides the massed precision fire. During the first night, waves of F-35As and F-35Cs enter Iranian airspace in small formations. Rather than immediately attacking dozens of strategic sites, they concentrate on opening corridors through Iran’s air defenses. Radars, command posts, surface-to-air missile sites and communications centers are struck first. Iranian operators face a dilemma. Every radar that activates risks revealing its position. Every battery that remains silent allows American fighters to penetrate farther. Within forty-eight hours, large portions of western Iranian airspace become increasingly dangerous for Iranian aircraft and air-defense crews. At the same time, American forces deploy HIMARS batteries across friendly territory surrounding Iran. The new concept becomes simple: F-35 detects. Network identifies. HIMARS fires. Launcher relocates. Iranian missile batteries, ammunition depots, airfields and IRGC headquarters near the western frontier are hit repeatedly. The Iranians quickly adapt. Ballistic missile launchers scatter into mountains and cities. Decoys appear beside highways. Commanders abandon fixed headquarters. Missile crews operate from tunnels and temporary firing positions. By Day Five, the war becomes a massive hunt. F-35s patrol above Iran searching for mobile launchers while HIMARS crews wait for targeting coordinates. Western Iran suffers heavily. Air-defense coverage fragments. Several major airfields become unusable. Logistics routes are repeatedly cut. Iranian units learn that remaining stationary for too long can be fatal. But Washington soon discovers the weakness of its self-imposed doctrine. HIMARS cannot reach much of central and eastern Iran. F-35s can strike deep targets, but they cannot replace heavy bombers carrying the largest bunker-penetrating weapons. Iran’s deepest underground nuclear and missile facilities therefore remain largely intact. The Pentagon changes tactics. Instead of trying to destroy underground complexes directly, F-35s attack their entrances, ventilation systems, electrical infrastructure, roads and communications. The objective becomes to seal Iran underground. By the second week, Epic Fury looks completely different from previous American wars. There are no enormous bomber raids or huge cruise-missile barrages. Instead, stealth fighters continuously hunt targets while mobile rocket batteries fire from distant positions and move before Iran can retaliate. Iran loses much of its exposed conventional infrastructure, but enough ballistic missiles and underground facilities survive to prolong the conflict. Tehran claims that America failed to destroy Iran’s strategic core. Washington argues that Iranian air defenses, bases and surface forces have been systematically dismantled. Neither side achieves a clean victory. Operation Epic Fury eventually becomes famous as the first major American campaign built almost entirely around a stealth sensor-shooter network. Military academies summarize the doctrine in four lines: F-35 finds. HIMARS fires. Iran hides. America hunts again. The lesson is clear: Against exposed forces, Lightning and Thunder is devastating. Against a country built around mountains, tunnels and buried facilities, even the most advanced precision network cannot solve every problem.

story-640125bfa12ff4d4ba67e136.content: 🇺🇸⚔️🇮🇷On the US military contingent in the Middle East It has been nearly six months since the start of Operation "Epic Fury," yet Washington continues to hotly debate its ultimate objective. Regardless, there is still no sign of clear de-escalation. The deployment of US forces within the operation zone serves as direct confirmation of this. What is happening in various parts of the operation zone? ▪️Three carrier strike groups are operating in the Arabian Sea, led by the *George H.W. Bush*, the *Abraham Lincoln*, and the newly arrived *George Washington*. The *George Washington* is slated to replace the *Lincoln*, resulting in a period where three aircraft carriers are present in the area simultaneously. They are escorted by the cruisers *Princeton* and *Richard S. Edwards*, as well as nine guided-missile destroyers. ▪️Additionally, the task force includes the amphibious assault ship *Boxer* and the amphibious transport docks *Portland* and *Comstock*. This maintains the US capability to rapidly deploy equipment and supplies to the Persian Gulf region. ▪️The destroyer *Gonzalez* is operating in the Red Sea. Four other guided-missile ships are located in the Gulf of Aden, between Yemen and the Maldives. Their primary missions involve protecting shipping and intercepting missiles, drones, and unmanned surface vessels belonging to the Sana'a-based Ansarallah movement. ▪️In the Mediterranean, the destroyer *Paul Ignatius* is operating near Cyprus, maintaining a presence off the eastern Mediterranean coast. The *Franklin D. Roosevelt* has moved further west to the area of ​​Souda Bay, Crete. If necessary, both ships can launch cruise missiles at targets in western Iran. ▪️ Over the past 24 hours, US and Israeli tactical aircraft conducted 29 sorties over Syria and Iraq for combat patrols near the Iranian border. Additionally, three E-11A communications aircraft flew from Prince Sultan Air Base, maintaining stable communications for the US force contingent. ▪️ Seven US aircraft and six drones were deployed for reconnaissance missions. The airspace over Iran was also monitored by three Turkish Bayraktar TB2s and one Akinci drone operating from southeastern Turkey. There have been no significant qualitative changes to the force grouping since mid-August: no new wave of bombers has arrived, and the naval composition is changing only through routine rotation. However, the US currently enjoys a temporary boost in capabilities due to the presence of three aircraft carriers, maintaining a high tempo of reconnaissance, patrolling, and situational monitoring near Iran's borders. All this is taking place against the backdrop of Trump's promises to launch the "largest economic operation" against Iran. So far, these bold words have been backed primarily by familiar sanctions, while the military force grouping remains the actual instrument of pressure. Yet, this force is stretched thin between the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, making it difficult to simultaneously pressure the Iranians and contain Yemen's Ansarallah movement. rybar

story-66660f570dda3b5048006048.content: The anti-AI revolt is here, writes @phil_tinline If the AI roll-out amounts to a social and economic revolution, then we must prepare for the political reaction bound to follow, but which few in the political world understand. The “techlash” has already begun, and it may yet prove as transformative for world politics as the technology itself claims to be. Put your ear to the ground and under all the noisy enthusiasm a shift is already audible. In March last year, the Ada Lovelace Institute – which is dedicated to ensuring that AI works for those of us who don’t run tech companies – found that concern around how AI would be used had increased “significantly” since its first study in 2022-23, when ChatGPT was launched. In a further study last December, the same institute found that 84 per cent of the public believed the government put the interests of Big Tech ahead of their own. And that was before January’s torrent of sexualised deepfakes, generated from images of real people with the help of Elon Musk’s AI service Grok, and the growing controversy around Palantir, the data analysis firm that works with Ice in the US, the Israeli defence ministry and the NHS. According to one parliamentary aide, public disquiet about both companies’ behaviour has been landing in MPs’ in-trays. The public’s objections to the AI revolution are widespread and growing, from the copyright violations involved in training AI models – in which giant tech firms trawl through books, music, newspaper articles and so on to feed content into their large language models – to the environmental impact of data centres, and the semi-autonomous weapons systems being used on the front lines in Ukraine and in Gaza. AI slop pervades social media and, increasingly, every other form of media, from film to music, journalism and even books. There is also mounting concern about the racial bias in AI facial recognition technology, the dangers of driverless vehicles and the potential destruction of vast swathes of productive work. Beyond all that lurks the most frightening spectre of all: the prospect of handing extortionists, terrorists and dictators the means to hack into our critical infrastructure; to control military hardware and create bioweapons; even to launch wars. Oh, and of course, the threat of turning humanity into one great Dr Frankenstein, as we lose control of our superintelligent creation altogether. https://t.co/Nd9WZBhzMp

story-6831a7d03458348724b159d3.content: Combat Drones: Enhancing, Not Replacing, Attack Helicopters Modern combat drones are changing warfare and exposing gaps in international law. They are not replacing attack helicopters or fighter jets. Instead, they are being used alongside them to improve missions, reduce risks for pilots, and make military operations more effective. As this technology advances, international law must also keep pace. Drone technology is evolving much faster than international arms control laws. Modern drones are no longer limited to surveillance. They can carry precision-guided weapons, destroy tanks, suppress enemy air defences, and perform many missions once carried out by attack helicopters and fighter jets. After the Ukraine war, many militaries began investing in AI-powered combat drones because they are cheaper, more flexible, and reduce the risk to pilots. Systems such as the Anduril Thunder, Bayraktar Kizilelma, FH-97A, GJ-11 Sharp Sword, and Russia's S-70 Okhotnik demonstrate this shift. Countries including Japan and the United Kingdom are also expanding their drone capabilities. The United States has introduced the Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA), or Loyal Wingman programme, where an F-35 works with several AI-powered drones. The pilot directs the mission while the drones enter dangerous areas, locate enemy air defences, and engage targets. China and Russia are developing similar systems with their J-20, Su-57, and autonomous combat drones, showing that human-machine teamwork is becoming central to future air warfare. However, international arms control has not kept up. Existing treaties mainly regulate manned aircraft, while armed drones often fall into legal grey areas, allowing them to be traded and deployed with fewer restrictions. Artificial intelligence has created another challenge. Some drones can continue missions and identify targets even after losing contact with their operators. International Humanitarian Law requires humans to make decisions about the use of lethal force, but there is still no clear legal responsibility if an autonomous drone mistakenly attacks civilians. It remains uncertain whether responsibility lies with the commander, manufacturer, or software developer. This issue is now a major debate at the United Nations under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW). Many countries want rules banning fully autonomous weapons without meaningful human control, while allowing limited use under strict conditions. However, the United States, Russia, China, and Israel argue that existing international law is enough and oppose a binding treaty. Because new UN rules require consensus, no new global agreement has been reached. Another debate focuses on Meaningful Human Control. Many experts believe a human should always make the final decision to use lethal force. Others support AI selecting targets while humans supervise. Critics warn that if communication is lost, these systems could become fully autonomous, allowing algorithms to make life-and-death decisions. Combat drones are transforming modern warfare, but they are not replacing attack helicopters or fighter jets. Instead, they are making them more capable and effective. As military technology continues to evolve, international law must evolve as well to address the legal, ethical, and security challenges of autonomous warfare. #Drones

story-6b5ebf02bba5d2da7ecb3897.content: 🚨 CHINA’S MILITARY LEANED ON U.S. AI MODELS, NEW REPORT SAYS. A new report says Chinese military researchers have quietly used U.S. artificial intelligence models to build their own defense systems. Analysts reviewed more than 80 Chinese papers and patents published between 2024 and 2026. They found repeated use of “model distillation,” a method that takes outputs from a powerful AI and uses them to train a smaller one. The study links this work to units inside the People’s Liberation Army. Researchers used U.S. models to process code, generate training data, and compress image‑analysis tools for drones and other hardware. The report says these distilled systems help China bypass limits on advanced chips and speed up development of military AI. U.S. officials argue this practice skirts export controls and infringes on intellectual property. China denies wrongdoing and says Washington is trying to block its technological rise. The findings add new tension ahead of talks on AI safety and governance, showing how both countries are racing to shape the future of military technology.

story-6d0853413b84a0a2b35918dc.content: إسرائيل تنفق ملايين الدولارات للتأثير على إجابات الذكاء الاصطناعي حول غزة كشف تحقيق نشرته منصة «دروب سايت نيوز» أن الحكومة الإسرائيلية تدفع 46.5 مليون دولار لشركة «كلوك تاور إكس» التي يديرها براد بارسكيل، المدير السابق لحملة دونالد ترامب الانتخابية، بهدف التأثير على إجابات أنظمة الذكاء الاصطناعي حول الحرب في غزة والعلاقات الأمريكية الإسرائيلية. شبكة مواقع مخصصة للآلات لا للقراء أنشأت الشركة شبكة من عشرة مواقع إلكترونية مثل «فاكت سيجنال» و«أليڤيا» و«باكس بوينت»، تنشر مئات المقالات التي تروج للرواية الإسرائيلية. هذه المواقع لا تستهدف القراء البشر، إذ لا يتجاوز زوار معظمها بضع مئات شهرياً، بل صُممت خصيصاً لتُلتقط من محركات البحث وأنظمة التدريب الخاصة بنماذج الذكاء الاصطناعي، في عملية يصفها الخبراء بـ«تسميم النماذج اللغوية الكبيرة». تأثير ملموس على الشات بوتات ووفقاً للتحقيق، بدأت هذه المواقع تظهر في إجابات أدوات مثل بيربلكسيتي ومايكروسوفت كوبايلوت وجيميني. فعندما سُئل بيربلكسيتي عن فائدة تعزيز التعاون العسكري الأمريكي مع إسرائيل، أجاب بكلمة واحدة: «نعم»، مستنداً إلى أحد مواقع بارسكيل كمصادر رئيسية. كما دخلت محتويات الشبكة في بيانات «كومن كرول» المستخدمة في تدريب معظم النماذج الكبرى، حيث سُجلت أكثر من 900 عملية زحف بين كانون الثاني وحزيران 2026. يُعد هذا الجهد جزءاً من حملة أوسع للتأثير على الرأي العام الأمريكي، ويُظهر كيف أصبحت أنظمة الذكاء الاصطناعي ساحة جديدة في الصراع على السرديات. https://t.co/O3ggZQNm2a

story-6dea4a469efcc7617b65d92a.content: Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense confirms that its forces now employ more than 70 AI and computer vision systems to strike enemy targets, with over 200 Ukrainian companies developing and manufacturing AI-powered drones. The effort runs through Brave1, the state defense innovation cluster, and it is deliberately international. The Brave1 Dataroom, where developers train military AI on real combat data, was built with the American company Palantir Technologies, while the BraveTech EU initiative launched with the European Union scales these military innovations across the continent. Europe is also supplying hardware. German defense technology company Helsing is producing 6,000 HX-2 strike drones for Ukraine, following an earlier order of 4,000 HF-1 drones built in partnership with Ukrainian industry, with onboard AI providing resistance to electronic warfare and jamming. The result is resilience. Drones lock onto targets and continue autonomously when Russian jamming cuts the operator link, though humans still make the final strike decision. story-6deec140a7a0bc5216328d78.content: Saildrone launched two Lockheed Martin JAGM missiles from its Surveyor unmanned surface vessel (USV) during RIMPAC 2026, marking the first missile launches from a Saildrone platform. The launches took place off Hawaii under the U.S. Navy’s Fleet Experimentation Program. The Surveyor operated alongside Carrier Strike Group 9 and used the Navy’s Adjunct Remote Engagement System (ARES) to engage a surrogate high-speed surface target. The Surveyor is a multi-mission USV designed for maritime ISR, deep-ocean mapping and long-endurance operations. Saildrone also tested a passive electronic warfare sensor during RIMPAC, which detected and identified a simulated threat radar. Saildrone said the decision to launch remained under human control and that the demonstration did not involve autonomous weapons. The company is also developing the larger Spectre USV, which measures 52 meters (170 ft) and is designed to carry larger, containerized mission payloads. Planned future capabilities include Lockheed Martin’s Mk 70 launcher and anti-submarine warfare systems. #Saildrone #Surveyor #JAGM #USV #RIMPAC2026 #LockheedMartin #UnmannedSystems #MaritimeDrones #NavalTechnology #DefenseTechnology

story-6f67f13d36f4fed02e3c6614.content: AI researcher Prof. Dr. Karl Hans Bläsius warns that humanity has already lost control over artificial intelligence. In a recent interview on the Everlast AI channel, the long-time AI expert (researching the field since 1981 and former professor of computer science at Hochschule Trier) delivers a stark assessment of AI’s trajectory — especially its military applications. Bläsius, author of the book KI und Krieg (“AI and War”), argues that the risks go far beyond typical concerns about job displacement or bias. Blasius is a researcher with 40+ years in the field: “We have already lost control.” He warns that autonomous weapons, AI-driven early-warning systems, and the race toward superintelligence have pushed us past the point of reliable human oversight. Accidental nuclear escalation, unstoppable cyber capabilities, and systems that can no longer be fully controlled are no longer theoretical risks. His core message: classical arms control doesn’t work on software. Only genuine international cooperation can still reduce the danger. #ArtificialIntelligence #AIRisks #AutonomousWeapons #Superintelligence #AIWarfare #ExistentialRisk #KarlHansBläsius #KIUndKrieg #ControlLoss #FutureOfAI

story-6f7feced9177efbf263f4d88.content: Policy Priority: NATIONAL SECURITY AND U.S. LEADERSHIP AI is now a front-line national security asset. The same advanced chips and models that drive American innovation can, in the wrong hands, accelerate cyberattacks, autonomous weapons, and the surveillance regimes of authoritarian rivals. Protecting that advantage is inseparable from using it responsibly. Maintaining American leadership means keeping our most advanced technology out of adversaries’ hands: enforcing export controls, closing the loopholes that let restricted chips slip through, and securing supply chains against theft and espionage. View all of our priorities: https://t.co/uPjsj4D9oc

story-70002a6dd9b56053e52081ba.content: 𝗔𝗹𝗴𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗺𝗶𝗰 𝗪𝗮𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗿𝗲, 𝗛𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗝𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗗𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗗𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 Attended a stimulating discussion as a panelist at the Observer Research Foundation seminar. It highlighted the debate on military AI is rapidly moving beyond technology to questions of doctrine, trust and strategic competition. Some key points brought out by me during the panel discussion: • 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗯𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼 𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗽, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗽. As decision cycles compress, tactical decisions may increasingly be delegated to machines, while humans focus on mission objectives, Rules of Engagement, escalation thresholds and political oversight. • 𝗧𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆. Future conflicts will depend not only on trust between humans and machines, but increasingly on trust between interconnected machine systems operating at machine speed. That trust must be earned through rigorous testing, validation and operational experience. • 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗰 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗲𝘁𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘂𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗴𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. Every nation supports responsible AI in principle, yet few are willing to slow military development if potential adversaries continue to advance. Strategic necessity is likely to remain the stronger driver. • 𝗗𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗗𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗳𝘂𝗹 𝗳𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗹𝗴𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗺𝗶𝗰 𝗪𝗮𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗿𝗲. AI is only one component. True decision dominance integrates sensors, communications, cyber, electronic warfare, logistics, command-and-control and human judgement into a coherent operational ecosystem. • 𝗔𝗹𝗴𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗺𝗶𝗰 𝘀𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗶𝗴𝗻𝘁𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗰 𝗻𝗲𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘆. Military advantage will increasingly depend on sovereign control over data, AI models, communications, cloud infrastructure, C2 systems, testing and continuous assurance—not merely access to AI applications. • 𝗖𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲, 𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗰𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗱𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝗔𝗜. The doctrine on which AI is trained, the authority delegated to machines and the allocation of responsibility for AI-enabled decisions will differ across nations and influence battlefield outcomes. The AI race in defence is therefore not simply about building smarter algorithms. It is about building trusted national decision ecosystems that can sense, understand, decide and act faster than an adversary—while preserving meaningful human responsibility where it matters most. @orfonline #ArtificialIntelligence #MilitaryAI #DecisionDominance #AlgorithmicWarfare #AutonomousSystems #DefenceTechnology #NationalSecurity #ORF #AIGovernance

story-7209109f4e310906b5f7205d.content: The Most Dangerous Weapon in a Democracy May Not Look Like a Weapon The recent CJP protest reveals how algorithms and platforms can be used in warfare in a democracy. I share below details of a hypothetical situation in which Indian democracy can be attacked using modern propaganda warfare! Most people imagine the future of warfare in physical terms: drones swarming cities, autonomous weapons, cyberattacks on power grids, or missiles guided by artificial intelligence. But to destabilize a democracy, an adversary need not destroy its physical infrastructure. It may only need to manipulate what its citizens collectively believe. An adversary need not be external only. It can also be internal, someone who is hungry for power at any cost. Now here is the scenario.. Imagine an election being announced. The government remains legally in power, but the Model Code of Conduct limits major new decisions, while every enforcement action is subjected to intense political scrutiny. The country enters a sensitive transition period in which institutions are cautious, parties are campaigning, and public attention is unusually malleable. At precisely this moment, a coordinated influence operation begins. Thousands—or eventually millions—of synthetic identities, automated accounts, and seemingly ordinary citizen profiles start circulating scripted stories. Some allegations may contain fragments of truth. Others may be distorted, selectively edited or entirely fabricated. Images are taken out of context. Old videos are presented as current events. Individual incidents are described as evidence of nationwide brutality or institutional collapse. No single post needs to convince anyone. In fact, most people may initially dismiss the claims. But then the same narrative appears again—from another account, in another language, through a different video and seemingly from an unrelated person. It receives thousands of likes and comments. Influencers begin discussing it. Journalists respond to the online “controversy.” Political leaders cite the media coverage, while social-media users cite the political reactions. The narrative manufactures its own evidence of importance. This is where psychology becomes more powerful than technology. Human beings often use repetition, social agreement and apparent popularity as shortcuts for judging credibility. When we encounter the same claim repeatedly, it begins to feel familiar; familiarity can then be mistaken for truth. When millions appear to agree, neutral observers begin to wonder whether they have overlooked something. The question slowly changes from: “Is this allegation true?” to: “Why are so many people talking about it?” and eventually: “Perhaps I was wrong all along.” This is not traditional propaganda, where a government broadcasts one message from a central source. It is the artificial construction of social consensus. The citizen does not feel that propaganda has been delivered to them. They feel that they have independently discovered what everyone else already knows. That is what makes it so effective. Earlier, foreign powers dropped pamphlets behind enemy lines. The origin of the message was visible, and its reach was limited. Today, digital platforms can deliver individualized narratives to millions of people within hours. One citizen may see stories about corruption, another about religious persecution, another about unemployment, and another about national security. Different emotional triggers can lead different groups toward the same political outcome. The objective need not be to make everyone believe one grand lie. It may be enough to: exhaust citizens until they no longer know whom to trust; turn isolated incidents into the appearance of a national pattern; provoke real protests through manufactured outrage; deepen existing social divisions; suppress enthusiasm among supporters of one side; create a widespread feeling that political change is inevitable. Once real people begin participating, the distinction between foreign propaganda, partisan campaigning and genuine public opinion becomes extremely difficult to identify. A manufactured narrative can produce authentic anger; that anger then creates real events, which provide fresh content for the original narrative. The operation becomes self-sustaining. In a country such as India, where many citizens spend several hours each day consuming content through social and messaging platforms, the speed and scale of such manipulation could be extraordinary. Linguistic diversity does not necessarily protect the country either. Generative AI can now produce persuasive messages, images, voices and videos across languages and local cultural contexts at minimal cost. This does not mean every protest, criticism or change in public opinion is foreign-engineered. Treating all dissent as propaganda would itself be dangerous and would allow governments to escape legitimate accountability. The real challenge is more subtle: protecting authentic democratic disagreement from covert, coordinated and artificially amplified manipulation. The defence therefore cannot be censorship alone. Governments deciding what is true can become as dangerous as private platforms secretly deciding what citizens should see. A democratic response requires transparency: clear identification of automated and synthetic accounts; disclosure of coordinated political advertising and sponsorship; independent audits of recommendation algorithms during elections; rapid exposure of coordinated inauthentic behaviour; verifiable provenance for high-impact audio and video; stronger public awareness of how repetition and apparent popularity influence belief. The most serious national-security question of the AI era may not be whether an enemy can invade our borders. It may be whether an enemy—or even a domestic political actor—can enter the information environment, manufacture the appearance of public opinion, and make citizens believe that a decision engineered for them was entirely their own. A missile can damage a city. A sufficiently powerful propaganda system can capture the decision-making process of an entire country—without firing a single shot.

Open weights Qwen 3.8-27B running on Mac can provide malware, fraud and weapons instructions) - Do not want US to sell powerful chips or chipmaking equipment to China. Without chips, China can’t use scaling laws to build more powerful AI models than US. - Want the competition between US companies only, then AI advancement pacing, safety or pause can be figured out. - Stop large scale distillation attacks on US AI models as it helps China catch up to US AI models - Want sufficiently capable models, open and closed, should go through mandatory safety testing. - Mostly agree with Nvidia’s Open Weights and American AI Leadership letter. - Don’t agree with Nvidia’s stance that open-weights models necessarily helps defenders more than attackers. Realistically addressing its risks is possible. - Country of geniuses in a data center (of powerful AIs) can operate faster than humans when they arrive. - Think country of geniuses can have their own goals, can act like mercenaries, lead to mass unemployment, global economic disruption, concentration of wealth and power.

story-74e8da77f714a05f7e9490c5.content: Surveillance State The Complete Control Grid — What It Looks Like When You Lay It All Out You've heard about Flock cameras. You've heard about data centers. But nobody has laid out the full picture — every piece, connected, showing what it looks like when you assemble it all together. This is that picture. THE NETWORK — PIECE BY PIECE Flock Safety — License Plate Readers Over 20 billion license plate scans per month. The Condor camera pans, zooms, and specifically tracks humans — not just plates. The CEO uses 3 cars, 3 routes, and 3 different plates so he can't be tracked by his own product. Flock's own words: "customers own and control the data." The customer is the government. That makes it a warrantless government seizure of your location data. AXON — The Body Camera Cloud Body cameras on every officer uploading in real time to AXON's federal cloud infrastructure. Facial recognition. Biometric databases. $220 million in federal contracts. The footage doesn't just stay local — it feeds a national database. Data Centers — The AI Processing Layer The infrastructure that makes mass behavioral profiling possible at scale. A single large facility consumes up to 5 million gallons of treated drinking water per day. The profits leave. The water bill stays. Without data centers, the rest of the network cannot function. Autonomous Drones — Eyes in the Sky Surveillance drones capable of facial recognition in testing and active deployment, license plate reading, and continuous area monitoring without a single officer on the ground. Some operate autonomously. No warrant. No officer. No accountability. Humanoid Robots & Ground Units — The Physical Layer Boston Dynamics and equivalent platforms. Boston Dynamics platforms have demonstrated speeds exceeding 28mph in controlled testing — with commercial deployment expanding rapidly. Deployable for crowd monitoring, perimeter control, and physical enforcement. The surveillance network doesn't stay digital. Geofencing — The Digital Perimeter Virtual boundaries that trigger automatic alerts when a specific device, license plate, or biometric signature enters a defined zone. You don't have to be doing anything wrong. You just have to be there. Stingrays — Cell Tower Simulators Devices that mimic cell towers and capture all communications — calls, texts, data — from every phone in a given area. No individual warrant required. Everyone in range is captured. Smart Meters — The Energy Profile Utility meters that record energy usage patterns in real time. When you're home. When you're not. What appliances you're running. Behavioral profiling through your power bill. Fusion Centers — Where It All Comes Together Federal and local data sharing hubs that aggregate Flock data, AXON data, drone footage, stingray captures, and smart meter profiles into unified citizen dossiers. 79 fusion centers operate across the United States. Lavender & "Where's Daddy" — The Targeting Architecture AI targeting systems documented by +972 Magazine and The Guardian in Gaza. Lavender identified human targets. "Where's Daddy" tracked when targets entered their family homes — to maximize kill efficiency. The same architectural framework. The same AI logic. Already tested. Already proven. Already exportable. WHAT THIS LOOKS LIKE ASSEMBLED This is not a collection of separate programs. It is a unified control grid with redundant layers. If one piece is challenged legally, the others continue. If one jurisdiction bans Flock, AXON picks up the slack. If drones are restricted, stingrays fill the gap. The network is designed to be legally resilient — meaning no single court victory dismantles it. Only a constitutional prohibition on the entire architecture does.

Jingan Technology, a Hangzhou-based defense AI firm, reportedly used AI and open-source intelligence to detect a major U.S. surveillance build-up in the Middle East more than 50 days before the strikes on Iran. Its Jingqi Global Situational Awareness System is positioned as a direct competitor to Palantir's Gotham and Anduril's Lattice, already deployed across PLA and state security units. Katrina Manson's Project Maven tells the American side of this story. A Marine colonel and a small team proved AI-enabled decision-making in combat, but only by operating as insurgents inside the Pentagon's own acquisition system. Eight years later, the capabilities Maven pioneered are operational across combatant commands and NATO. China's military-civil fusion strategy faces different constraints, but fewer of the institutional antibodies Manson describes so well. Fielding speed and operational trust will determine who holds the advantage. Our full review: https://t.co/sZXeM9Fse1

story-75b8ba4f223b320e63196b14.content: 🇺🇸 USA / GREENLAND | Oil, Trump and Golden Dome - the extraordinary story behind Greenland Energy Greenland Energy Company is a small U.S. exploration company that began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker GLND in March 2026. Its entire investment thesis revolves around the Jameson Land Basin in East Greenland, covering roughly two million acres. Through agreements with 80 Mile and White Flame Energy, Greenland Energy can earn up to a 70% working interest by funding exploration drilling. An independent Sproule ERCE assessment estimates approximately 13 billion barrels of gross unrisked prospective recoverable oil. Crucially, these are prospective resources - Greenland Energy currently has no proved commercial oil reserves and generates no oil-production revenue. The story becomes far more interesting when geopolitics enters the picture. Donald Trump has repeatedly argued that Greenland is critical to U.S. national security. In January, Trump explicitly said that “a piece” of America’s planned Golden Dome missile-defence architecture would be located in Greenland. The United States already operates Pituffik Space Base on the island, including powerful early-warning radar used to track missile threats across the Arctic. At the same time, Greenland Energy has aggressively pushed ahead with plans to drill for oil on the island. The company has links to figures in Trump’s political orbit, while Trump ally Dr Phil is producing a documentary series about the Greenland Energy expedition. Then came an especially striking connection. In June, Greenland Energy appointed Carol Craig to its board. Craig is the founder and CEO of Sidus Space. Sidus Space has been selected as an awardee under the U.S. Missile Defense Agency’s SHIELD contract vehicle. SHIELD forms part of the broader Golden Dome missile-defence strategy. Sidus says its satellite, computing and defence technologies are positioned to support Golden Dome requirements. That means the CEO of a company participating in America’s Golden Dome ecosystem now also sits on the board of the U.S. oil explorer attempting to establish a major presence in Greenland. Does this prove that oil exploration is merely a pretext for establishing Golden Dome infrastructure in Greenland? No. There is currently no evidence that Greenland Energy itself holds a Golden Dome contract or is acting as a front for U.S. military deployment. But the overlap is real: Trump wants Golden Dome infrastructure in Greenland, Washington wants greater strategic access to the island, and Greenland Energy now has a director whose other company participates directly in the Golden Dome defence ecosystem. Greenland’s government has also pushed back. Authorities said the project still lacked required approvals, and after controversy over equipment brought to the island, the planned drilling campaign was delayed. Greenland Energy and its partners are now targeting a permitting timeline extending into winter 2027. The setback sent another shock through the company’s share price. Greenland Energy stock today: Ticker: GLND Exchange: Nasdaq Current price: approximately $1.25 The shares reached an all-time high of $23.00 on March 26. On August 12 they hit an all-time low of $1.10. Current market capitalization is roughly $56 million. The eye-catching part is the analyst target. The currently published 12-month target is $10 per share. From a price of roughly $1.25, that would represent approximately 700% upside. But there is a major caveat: the forecast comes from only one analyst, ThinkEquity. It is not a broad Wall Street consensus. SEC filings also show that ThinkEquity previously had significant financial relationships with Greenland Energy. It served as an adviser around the company’s business combination, participated in financing activities and acted as sole placement agent for Greenland Energy’s $70 million public offering. story-7682a11976a3502463623d53.content: LOSING OUR MINDS For years, scientists have embarked on systematic research to illuminate how human-machine interactions affect cognition. The findings are complicated, but often worrying. For example, people can suffer from what is called automation bias: the tendency to defer to machine judgments over their own. This was true before the advent of AI; simply search for videos of people who blindly followed their navigation systems and drove their cars into lakes. AI could make automation bias worse. Analysts have found that relying on AI can impair skill development for new learners while degrading knowledge among experts. When researchers gave computer scientists and oncologists AI assistance and later took it away, both groups performed worse at their jobs than they did before using it. These findings should be particularly concerning to the U.S. military as it seeks to foster what Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth calls an “AI-first warfighting force.” Some commanders hope to use AI to support war game analysis and to help develop military courses of action. Such integration could lead to tactical and strategic breakthroughs, given how powerful AI models have become. But it also risks diminishing the ability of commanders and soldiers to independently evaluate or develop creative military options. It is easy to imagine how this might happen. Sailors, for example, are often tired and overworked when reviewing images of potential threats. If they are evaluating an image of a nearby object, they might already be ready to accept the verdict of a computer that deems it an enemy warship—even when their own eyes suggest it is more likely a cargo tanker or a fishing boat. Likewise, battlefield commanders often need urgent response plans to enemy attacks, something AI can help with. But if commanders overrely on what computers suggest, they might lose their own tactical edge and blindly adopt the algorithm’s plan. This possibility is particularly concerning given that, in some experiments, AI models have been prone to make unnecessarily aggressive and escalatory recommendations. Relying on AI can impair skill development. To some, these fears may seem outlandish. The U.S. military, after all, invests tremendous amounts of resources on making sure its members exercise good judgment. The process by which it selects senior combat leaders, for example, is designed to weed out all but the most experienced and discerning candidates. Once selected, these leaders adhere to a strict code of conduct and undergo intensive training and certification requirements, all of which prize discipline and self-regulation. Finally, the American military bureaucracy has been focused on safely operating automated (if not autonomous) weapons since at least the 1940s. https://t.co/FiaG2utB8l via @ForeignAffairs
