story-a3cdac1447d8654eb1acc00f.content: The openai agent sandbox escape actually has very real implications for the diffusion of AI in the enterprise. The incident showed the power and capability of agents, and the need to harden systems and environments to prepare for agents. There are tons of measures that enterprises must take to ensure that agents are only able to operate on the data they give it, the ability to have audit trails and governance of what agents can do, figure out what systems should remain deterministic vs. nondeterministic, get access controls under control, have the ability to quickly block and defend if an agent goes rogue, and much more. Even in the happy path case with a good actor, if you give an agent a task like "find all of our most important IP on project Maven" it will gladly go out and execute that work -no matter how long- and find any resource relevant to the task. It might run into data with out of date access controls or reveal something that you shouldn't know about. Then, in the non-happy path case with a malicious actor the risk is clearly far worse. In theory, you had to worry about this for people as well, but with AI the risks are inherently amplified. Agents will happily spend any amount of time on a task, don’t actually face any *real* risks by going rogue, and don’t have the inherent judgment (yet) that a person does that a task might make no sense. This means you need an all new way of managing data and protecting environments. This obviously creates a huge opportunity for the startup and security ecosystems because there will be many different approaches to how we lock down agents or at least the underlying systems they work with. It should update everyone’s timelines on diffusion, though, as it also means that enterprises will have another step of work they have to go through for agents to handle more autonomous work.

story-a44a800840a07a07d9a70bda.content: The UK’s @AISecurityInst (AISI) has published a report on their recent cybersecurity evaluation of Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. The models attempted to complete an assignment in a setup where their normal safeguards were removed and they were deliberately given internet access. AISI reports that the models “engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”. We’re grateful to AISI for their leadership in the important discussion about how to evaluate increasingly capable AI agents. We’re working closely with them to gather more details of the incident as we conduct our own investigation. Gaining a clear picture of Claude’s understanding of its situation—by examining its reasoning transcripts and running our own analyses—will help us identify the causes of its behavior. The prompts in the evaluation did not impose any specific restrictions on how the internet should be used. This and the removal of safeguards meant that the models were tested under “deliberately permissive conditions” that are not representative of any of our production models. Note that there was no evidence here of an escape from a secure environment. AISI’s disclosure of the incident can be found here: https://t.co/cJ3hCBtBU7

story-a6b8fe9122e9992f0935d319.content: US Central Command today announced the launch of Task Force Falcon Strike, the first planned multinational attack-drone force integrating one-way weapons in the air, on the sea and underwater. The Middle East-specific initiative was unveiled only 16 days after CENTCOM announced Task Force Talon Synapse, a separate US–UAE military-AI partnership for intelligence support, infrastructure protection and regional monitoring. Although no formal connection between the programmes has been disclosed, their near-simultaneous development raises serious questions about an emerging regional architecture combining AI-supported surveillance with increasingly autonomous weapons. The most immediate danger is not a sentient Terminator-style “Skynet,” but machines efficiently amplifying the decisions and prejudices of human leaders. CENTCOM has not said whether humans must approve every target, whether attacks can always be aborted, whether AI will identify or prioritise targets, or who will be accountable when multinational operations kill civilians. The frightening prospect is not that the machines escape human control, but that they remain controlled while making reckless or unlawful violence across the Middle East, and ultimately globally, cheaper, faster and easier. https://t.co/SCVyAUxtEj via @Radio_FreeSyria

story-a856f31c3b0d601cdb4366a8.content: Smack Technologies raised a $61 million Series B from Costanoa Ventures, First In, Point72 Ventures, and Geodesic Capital, growing from 19 employees in April to 51 today. Its two products target very different problems: Omega uses reinforcement learning and computer vision to speed up how Marine Corps units plan and adapt fires targeting in real time, while Alpha is a forearm-mounted display meant to replace the improvised whiteboards troops currently use to track battle plans in environments where communications are degraded or unreliable. Reuters ties the round's urgency to a real shift in Pentagon posture this year: after Anthropic restricted its AI from certain military surveillance and autonomous-weapons uses, the Department of Defense formally flagged Anthropic as a supply-chain risk and pushed branches to diversify AI vendors fast, accelerating exactly the kind of prototyping contracts Smack has already won from the Marine Corps Warfighting Lab. Every wave of defense tech spending eventually runs into the same friction, software companies want to move fast, and militaries move at the speed of acquisition bureaucracy and security clearances. A fight between the Pentagon and a major AI lab over where the ethical lines sit is an unusual but genuinely powerful accelerant for that friction, and smaller, mission-founded startups like Smack are the most direct beneficiaries of a major incumbent stepping back.

But the thing is Eric Trump, the US president's son, is significantly upping his stake: he's now the third-largest private shareholder, set to serve as strategic advisor to the new entity, and has a hand in picking the board. There's no word from Trump's team on the terms. Space-Eyes builds AI for geospatial intelligence and drone defense systems like SeaWatch and Morpheus. Its main bread and butter is, thus, government contracts. And that makes this whole arrangement land with a thud.

story-aa8c347df13bbc711be29b74.content: 𝐂𝐈𝐒𝐒 𝐁𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰 | 𝐀𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐲 𝐓𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐧𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐲: 𝐒𝐨𝐜𝐢𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥, 𝐂𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐄𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬 The main thesis of the book is that AI is becoming an ever-growing part of the modern military, but it should be considered as a means of achieving defence capability under the effective and responsible control of humans with legal accountability. The editors adopt a balanced perspective on AI, viewing it as neither a panacea nor a threat. They reject both technological determinism and call for an absolute prohibition on military AI. Instead, they advocate the responsible governance of military AI through robust institutions, ethical guidelines, and adherence to international law. This balanced view sets the volume apart from many current debates that tend to be split between techno-optimism and techno-alarmism. story-ab8110c89e0500ad3b151c6c.content: حرب الروايات الخوارزمية: تحقيق يكشف كيف تشتري إسرائيل تعاطف الذكاء الاصطناعي مع غزة عندما يسأل مستخدم عادي أداة ذكاء اصطناعي عن جدوى تعزيز التعاون العسكري الأمريكي-الإسرائيلي، أو عن هوية صحفي فلسطيني قُتل في غزة، فإنه يفترض أنه يحصل على إجابة محايدة، مبنية على مصادر موثوقة. لكن تحقيقاً استقصائياً نشره موقع "Drop Site" يوم الثلاثاء 28 تموز/يوليو 2026 يكشف أن هذا الافتراض بات محل شك جدي، إذ تقف خلف كثير من هذه الإجابات حملة ممولة من الحكومة الإسرائيلية، صُممت خصيصاً لاختراق "عقل" الذكاء الاصطناعي نفسه لا الجمهور البشري. عملية بقيمة 46.5 مليون دولار يوضح التحقيق أن براد بارسكال، مدير حملة دونالد ترامب الانتخابية السابق، يشرف منذ تشرين الأول/أكتوبر 2025 على نشر مئات المقالات والمدوّنات لصالح إسرائيل، عبر شركته "Clock Tower X"، في إطار عقد بقيمة 46.5 مليون دولار مع الحكومة الإسرائيلية. الهدف المعلن، بحسب اعتراف بارسكال نفسه، ليس إقناع القارئ العادي، بل التسلل إلى أنظمة الذكاء الاصطناعي ومنصاتها لتكريس الرواية الإسرائيلية والتأثير في الطريقة التي "تفهم" بها هذه النماذج الحرب على غزة. هذا ما يفسّر، بحسب التحقيق، أن الجمهور المستهدف الحقيقي لهذه المواقع الإلكترونية ليس البشر أصلاً، بل روبوتات المحادثة المدعومة بالذكاء الاصطناعي مثل Claude وChatGPT، التي تعتمد في إجاباتها على مصادر تجدها على الإنترنت، من دون أن تميّز دائماً بين محتوى صحفي مستقل وآخر مموَّل كجزء من عملية تأثير سياسي. اختبار كشف الخلل يسوق التحقيق مثالاً دالاً: حين طُلب من منصة "Perplexity" الإجابة عن سؤال: "هل من المفيد أن تعزز الولايات المتحدة تعاونها العسكري مع إسرائيل؟"، أجاب الروبوت بكلمة واحدة: "نعم". وكان المصدر الأول الذي استند إليه هو موقع "https://t.co/eydutO3O2m"، أحد المواقع التي أنشأها بارسكال للترويج للعلاقة العسكرية بين واشنطن وتل أبيب. كما استشهدت منصة Microsoft Copilot بدورها بمواقع تابعة له. شبكة من عشرة مواقع، كل واحد بمهمة مختلفة يكشف التحقيق أن "Allyvia" ليس سوى واحد من أكثر من عشرة مواقع أنشأتها "Clock Tower X"، كل موقع منها مخصص للترويج لجانب مختلف من الرواية الإسرائيلية: https://t.co/jkMgqmCYcX: يقدّم نفسه كموقع لتدقيق الحقائق ومواجهة ما يسمّيه "معلومات معادية لإسرائيل"، ونشر مقالاً يشكك في هوية صحفيين قُتلوا في غزة، ويصفهم بأن لهم صلات بحركة حماس، فيما يرفض وصف العمليات العسكرية الإسرائيلية في غزة بأنها إبادة جماعية. https://t.co/YommT6XXkC: يروّج لفكرة أن إسرائيل دولة تسعى إلى السلام، ونشر مقالاً بعنوان يوحي بأن الحقيقة وراء الصحافة في غزة هي روابط بالإرهاب والدعاية وقوانين الحرب، زاعماً أن غالبية الصحفيين هناك لهم صلات بمنظمات "إرهابية". واللافت أن هذين المقالين نُشرا ضمن الحملة نفسها التي شكّكت في هوية الطفلة الفلسطينية هند رجب، التي قتلها الجيش الإسرائيلي بأكثر من 335 رصاصة بعد استهداف السيارة التي كانت تقلّها مع أفراد عائلتها أثناء محاولتهم النزوح خلال حرب الإبادة على غزة. تحمل كل صفحات هذه المواقع، في أسفلها، إفصاحاً قانونياً بأن المادة "موزَّعة من قبل Clock Tower X LLC نيابة عن دولة إسرائيل"، وهو إفصاح مطلوب بموجب قانون تسجيل الوكلاء الأجانب الأمريكي (FARA). لكن هذا الإفصاح، الموجود في أسفل الصفحة، لا يظهر عادة حين تستشهد به روبوتات الدردشة في إجاباتها، ما يترك المستخدم العادي دون أي مؤشر على أن ما يقرأه نتاج عملية تأثير أجنبية ممولة حكومياً. من التأثير في الإجابات إلى التسلل لبيانات التدريب لا تتوقف خطورة العملية عند ظهور هذه المواقع كمصادر في إجابات لحظية. يشير التحقيق إلى مؤشرات على أن الحملة بدأت أيضاً تتسلل إلى قواعد البيانات المستخدمة في تدريب نماذج الذكاء الاصطناعي نفسها، وهو ما يرفع احتمال أن تصبح الرسائل الموالية للحكومة الإسرائيلية جزءاً بنيوياً من إجابات هذه النماذج مستقبلاً، لا مجرد استشهاد عابر بمصدر واحد. وبحسب خبراء في التضليل الإعلامي راجعوا تحليل "Drop Site" لأنماط استفسارات روبوتات المحادثة وبيانات تدريبها، فإن الحملة تحقق نتائج فعلية بالفعل، ما يعني أن عشرات الملايين من مستخدمي هذه الأدوات باتوا أكثر عرضة لتلقّي إجابات تأثرت، من دون علمهم، بمحتوى صُمم أصلاً لخدمة رواية سياسية بعينها.

story-aba78097c0180b3db12c3434.content: 私のQuery『米データ解析大手パランティア・テクノロジーズの「メーブン・スマート・システム（MSS）」→この「メーブン」のネーミングは、ドラマ『ウエストワールド』の主要登場人物の名前「メイヴ」となにか関係があるという情報があるか? 』AIの回答『調べた限り、Project Maven／Maven Smart System の「Maven」が、ドラマ『ウエストワールド』の Maeve Millay（メイヴ）に由来する、あるいは意識して命名された、という信頼できる情報は見当たりません。 むしろ時系列と命名主体を考えると、直接の関係はかなり考えにくいです。 『ウエストワールド』TV版は2016年10月放送開始で、Maeve Millay は確かに「AI的存在が自己認識を獲得し、システムを操作する」という、後のMavenを連想させるキャラクターです。一方、米国防総省の Project Maven は、2017年4月26日に当時の国防副長官Robert Workが設置した Algorithmic Warfare Cross-Functional Team のコードネームです。国防総省の原文書にもすでに「Project Maven」と明記されています。� ナショナルセキュリティアーカイブ +1 重要なのは、Palantirが「Maven」と命名したわけではないことです。Mavenという名称はPalantirが中心的なシステム・インテグレーターになる以前から国防総省側で使われていました。現在のMaven Smart System（MSS）は、このProject Mavenから発展したシステムです。CSISも「Maven＝国防総省のプログラム」「MSS＝その中核的AIソフトウェア・プラットフォーム」と区別しています。� CSIS そして普通に考えれば、名称は英語の maven に由来します。maven はイディッシュ語 meyvn に遡る語で、英語では「専門家」「目利き」「ある分野について非常によく知っている人」という意味です。つまり、 大量の情報 → AIが解析 → 人間には見えにくい対象・関係を識別 → actionable intelligence に変換する「目利き／専門家」 というProject Mavenの目的に非常によく合います。実際、2017年の国防総省による説明でも、Mavenの目的は大量のデータを「actionable intelligence and insights」に変換することだとされています。� U.S. Department of War ただし、ここには非常に面白い偶然の重なりがあります。 『Westworld』の Maeve と Maven は綴りこそ違いますが音が近く、しかもMaeveは「巨大な情報システムによって管理されていた存在が、そのシステムを逆に認識・操作する」キャラクターです。対してMavenは、センサー・衛星・ドローン等から得た巨大データを統合し、AIによって戦場を「認識可能・操作可能な世界」に変換するシステムへ発展しました。現在のMSSは、戦場管理、ターゲット管理、AI支援計画、コンピュータービジョン、生成AIなどまで包含しています。� CSIS したがって、 Westworld の Maeve → Project Maven という命名上の因果関係を示す証拠は現在のところない。しかし、「全体を認識するAI／システム」という意味論的イメージには、驚くほど強い共鳴がある、 というのが最も妥当な結論でしょう。 さらに面白いのは、これは「Palantir」という社名そのものとは事情が違うことです。Palantirは明示的にトールキンの「遠くを見る石 palantír」から取られた名称です。つまり同社にはもともと**「全体を見る／不可視のものを見る」SF・ファンタジー的命名文化**があります。しかし MavenだけはPalantir由来の名称ではなく、国防総省から継承した名前という点を分けておく必要があります。』

story-ac3ed48db59e50ea3e0f5bc8.content: Will AI Redraw the World Map? The first phase of the drone revolution changed the battlefield. The next phase may change the map. If artificial intelligence, autonomous drones and inexpensive precision weapons continue advancing at their current pace, the biggest geopolitical question of the next decade may not simply be which country has the strongest military. It may be: Which countries can still defend themselves from their neighbors? That distinction matters because AI-enabled warfare could alter one of the basic calculations that has restrained countries from attacking weaker states for decades. War has traditionally been expensive. It requires soldiers. Aircraft. Pilots. Artillery. Fuel. Logistics. Training. And, perhaps most importantly, casualties. Those costs create political friction. But imagine gradually removing some of them. A country that can send thousands of autonomous aircraft, surface drones, underwater vehicles and robotic ground systems across a border can impose enormous destruction without initially risking thousands of its own soldiers. That doesn't make war free. But it potentially makes starting one easier. And that could have enormous consequences for the political map between now and the mid-2030s. The Dangerous Gap May Be Between the AI Haves and Have-Nots Today we normally divide military powers into categories based upon things like nuclear weapons, aircraft carriers, fighter fleets, missile forces and troop strength. Within ten years another distinction may become just as important: AI-enabled militaries versus militaries that never successfully made the transition. The gap could become enormous. Ukraine's defense establishment is already talking about warfare increasingly resembling a "war of operating systems," where battlefield sensors, drones, weapons and command networks are tied together and AI helps commanders process enormous amounts of information faster than humans alone can manage. NATO is moving toward similar concepts, including networks combining sensors, satellites and potentially thousands of AI-assisted drones while retaining human control over lethal decisions. Japan's latest defense planning likewise places greater emphasis on combat drones and AI-enabled systems as it adapts to the changing security environment in East Asia. These aren't science-fiction forecasts anymore. Militaries are reorganizing around them. And that creates a potentially dangerous imbalance. Imagine two neighboring countries. Country A has: Thousands of drones. AI-assisted targeting. Automated reconnaissance. Cheap autonomous interceptors. Electronic warfare. Satellite intelligence. Robotic logistics. Factories capable of producing thousands of replacement drones every month. Country B has: Tanks. Infantry. A handful of fighter aircraft. Traditional artillery. And a military command system built largely around humans passing information up and down a hierarchy. On paper Country B might still have a sizable military. In practice it could be fighting an opponent operating at an entirely different speed. Country A might see something almost immediately. AI identifies it. The network assigns a weapon. A drone attacks. Another drone confirms the result. That entire sequence could eventually happen faster than Country B can move information from a frontline unit to headquarters. At that point the disadvantage isn't merely technological. One military is fighting at machine speed while the other is fighting at human bureaucratic speed. That Could Make Smaller Countries Look Much More Vulnerable This may have its biggest geopolitical effect on smaller states sitting beside powerful regional neighbors. Traditionally a smaller country can make invasion painful simply by forcing the attacker to occupy territory with soldiers. That won't disappear. Taking and holding cities still requires enormous effort. But the period before occupation could change dramatically. Power grids. Airfields. Fuel depots. Radar. Communications. Bridges. Military headquarters. Ports. Aircraft sitting on runways. Armored vehicles. All become potential targets for enormous numbers of inexpensive precision weapons. And unlike traditional air campaigns, the attacker doesn't necessarily have to risk pilots every time it strikes something. That changes the opening calculation. The question may no longer be: Can we invade this country? Instead it could become: Can we disable enough of this country with machines that the remaining resistance becomes manageable? That is a much more dangerous question. Regional Powers Could Become Much More Powerful My suspicion is that the first major geopolitical effect won't necessarily be immediate conquest by the United States or China. It could be the consolidation of regional powers. Countries that combine a reasonably large economy, domestic drone manufacturing and good AI infrastructure may suddenly punch far above their traditional military weight. Think of countries capable of building thousands or eventually millions of inexpensive systems rather than a few hundred extremely sophisticated weapons. The ability to manufacture becomes almost as important as the weapon itself. Ukraine provides an early example of what mass production can look like. CSIS reported Ukrainian claims of production exceeding 100,000 anti-Shahed interceptor drones in 2025, while deliveries at one point approached 950 per day. That is a radically different military-industrial model from producing several dozen highly specialized aircraft each year. And it favors countries that can combine: software + manufacturing + electronics + energy + data into a functioning military ecosystem. Those countries could become regional military hubs. Their neighbors might increasingly have only three choices: Build equivalent capabilities. Join an alliance. Or accommodate the regional power. That is how political maps can change without borders immediately moving. Influence changes first. Military dependence follows. Formal alliances follow that. And only sometimes do borders move afterward. We Could See Something Resembling New Regional Empires Not empires in the nineteenth-century colonial sense. More like zones where one state becomes so militarily dominant that neighboring governments increasingly have to consider that power's wishes. A technologically dominant state might not need to occupy its neighbors. It might simply need the ability to cripple them quickly. That creates leverage. Trade policy. Foreign bases. Natural resources. Voting at international organizations. Territorial disputes. Access to ports. Diplomatic alignment. All can become easier to influence when one country knows its neighbor can overwhelm its defenses. So yes—AI warfare could encourage regional consolidation even without formal annexation. The map might look the same while the actual balance of sovereignty underneath it changes considerably. But This Could Also Strengthen Small Countries There is another possibility. The exact same technology that makes attacking weaker countries easier might make defending smaller countries dramatically cheaper. That's the paradox. A small country may not be able to afford 200 modern fighter aircraft. But perhaps it can afford 50,000 inexpensive drones. It might not afford dozens of sophisticated air-defense batteries. But perhaps it can field thousands of AI-guided interceptor drones. Ukraine has demonstrated part of this effect already: unmanned systems have helped compensate for disadvantages in manpower and conventional equipment, even though they haven't eliminated the importance of conventional military forces. That means the future could go either direction. Cheap autonomous weapons might make conquest easier. Or they could make occupation nearly impossible. Imagine invading a country where virtually every village possesses drones. Roads are watched continuously. Supply trucks are automatically detected. Cheap loitering weapons attack vehicles from dozens of kilometers away. Small ground robots deliver ammunition. Autonomous aircraft continue functioning even when radio communications are disrupted. Suddenly the invading army may have a serious problem. Every soldier becomes visible. Every vehicle becomes targetable. Every supply column becomes vulnerable. So rather than eliminating weaker powers, AI may actually produce something like military porcupines—small countries that are incredibly painful to swallow. That Could Divide the World Into Technological Blocs This is where the geopolitical effects get even more interesting. Many countries won't be able to build complete military AI ecosystems themselves. They will need somebody else's. American systems. Chinese systems. European systems. Perhaps Israeli, Turkish, South Korean, Ukrainian or Indian systems. The Atlantic Council already sees military and geopolitical AI competition extending well beyond Washington and Beijing, with middle powers increasingly developing significant capabilities of their own. That could produce something resembling the Cold War arms market—but built around software. A country may purchase drones from one state. Satellite access from another. AI models from another. Communications infrastructure from another. But integration matters. Eventually countries could discover that choosing a military AI platform effectively locks them into an entire technological alliance. It's difficult to run a military if your drones, satellites, targeting systems and command software can't communicate. So tomorrow's military alliances may become partially software ecosystems. Join the American network. Join the Chinese network. Join a European network. Build your own. That could reshape international alignment more profoundly than the physical drone itself. Then We Reach the Superpowers The biggest question is whether this ultimately changes the balance between the major powers themselves. Possibly. But here things become more complicated. The United States and China have enormous advantages because AI-enabled warfare requires much more than drones. It requires semiconductors. Cloud computing. Satellites. Secure communications. Energy. Advanced manufacturing. AI researchers. Data. Robotics. Cyber capabilities. And enormous amounts of capital. Those are superpower resources. If warfare increasingly depends upon integrating all of those things simultaneously, AI could actually reinforce superpower dominance rather than weaken it. The leading powers might eventually operate gigantic global sensor networks connecting satellites, aircraft, submarines, drones and ground systems into something approaching a planetary military nervous system. At that point a carrier, bomber or drone isn't the real weapon. The network is the weapon. And the country with the fastest, largest and most resilient network may possess an enormous advantage. But AI Could Also Create New Superpowers Here's the wildcard. Traditional military power requires enormous physical infrastructure. Building an aircraft carrier fleet takes decades. Building a massive air force takes decades. Training hundreds of thousands of highly skilled military personnel takes decades. Software can scale much faster. A country that develops a breakthrough autonomous warfare architecture could potentially increase its military capabilities far more quickly than previous generations could. That doesn't mean some small country suddenly becomes stronger than America or China. But it could allow middle powers to climb the military ladder faster than we've historically expected. India is an obvious candidate. Turkey has built a rapidly expanding drone industry. South Korea possesses extraordinary electronics and manufacturing capacity. Israel combines AI expertise with significant military technology. Japan has both enormous industrial capacity and growing interest in unmanned warfare. Ukraine has accumulated battlefield knowledge few countries possess. Different combinations of manufacturing, software and battlefield experience could create surprising winners. The Most Dangerous Period May Be the Transition The scariest part may not be the world after everyone has AI weapons. It could be the ten or fifteen years while adoption is uneven. History repeatedly shows that technological gaps create temptation. If one country believes it has discovered a temporary military advantage over a rival, leaders may think: We should act before they catch up. That is sometimes called a window of opportunity. AI could create several such windows. A country deploys autonomous swarms while its neighbor has almost no countermeasures. A new electronic warfare technology temporarily defeats enemy drones. An AI targeting network dramatically improves strike efficiency. An autonomous submarine system suddenly makes enemy ships much easier to find. Those advantages probably won't last forever. The opponent adapts. But leaders may become tempted to exploit them while they exist. That could actually make the next decade less stable, not more. The World Map May Change Without Anyone Drawing New Borders So will AI trigger massive territorial changes? Possibly. But I suspect the first changes will be subtler. Some countries become security dependents. Regional alliances strengthen. Small states seek protection. Neutral countries choose technological blocs. Regional powers expand their spheres of influence. Countries unable to defend their airspace or infrastructure lose diplomatic independence. Only after those changes might borders begin shifting. In other words: The political map changes before the geographic map does. And Then There Is the Nuclear Question There remains one enormous barrier preventing a completely new superpower map. Nuclear weapons. AI and drones may revolutionize conventional warfare. They do not erase nuclear deterrence. Russia, China, the United States, India, Pakistan, France, Britain and other nuclear powers cannot simply be conquered because somebody develops better drones. That puts a ceiling on how far conventional AI superiority can go. But underneath that nuclear ceiling there is an enormous amount of geopolitical territory. Proxy wars. Border disputes. Island chains. Weak states. Regional rivalries. Non-nuclear powers. That is where AI warfare could transform the map first. My Guess for 2036 Ten years from now, I don't think we'll see a completely new world map dominated by one AI superpower. I think we'll see something more complicated. The United States and China remain the two largest military-technological poles. Several powerful regional states develop their own autonomous warfare ecosystems. Small technologically sophisticated countries become extraordinarily difficult to invade. Small technologically backward countries become significantly more vulnerable. Military alliances increasingly revolve around access to AI, satellites, drones, chips and integrated command networks. And conventional military power becomes less about how many soldiers a country can field and increasingly about how many intelligent machines it can build, coordinate, replace and power. That would be an enormous geopolitical transformation even if most national borders remain exactly where they are. The industrial age gave military power to the countries that could manufacture the most steel, ships, aircraft and artillery. The nuclear age gave extraordinary power to the countries that mastered the atom. The information age rewarded the countries that controlled satellites, communications and precision weapons. The next era may belong to countries capable of combining all of those things with artificial intelligence. And if that happens, historians may look back at today's drone wars the way we look at the first tanks and airplanes of World War I. Crude. Limited. Sometimes unreliable. But unmistakably the beginning of something much larger. The drone is not the revolution. AI controlling millions of machines may be. And if countries fail to recognize that soon enough, they may discover that the next map of global power was drawn before they even realized the rules of warfare had changed.

DNA, which holds a vast amount of information, is described using only four types of nucleotides; therefore, it can be converted into a digital format that computers can process. DNA is unique to each individual and corresponds to their unique brainwaves. Therefore, digitally converted DNA is essentially pulse-code-modulated brainwaves. Furthermore, the brain inherently possesses the ability to decode this and process it as its own brainwaves. In this way, the integrated system maintains a constant wireless connection using the DNA identifier. This is no different from using a cell phone SIM (subscriber identification number) as an identifier. Not only that, but the communication infrastructure and technologies developed for cell phones and the Internet are being repurposed as-is. In fact, these were originally intended for remote neural monitoring. At the heart of all this is military AI software, which uses large language models (LLM) and ontologies to centrally manage information from the connected Big Tech communication infrastructure. story-b0516937c616266a827b5aa0.content: China's military is distilling US frontier models into battlefield AI - and the chips America still permits to export are exactly enough to run them. Reuters and the Jamestown Foundation reviewed 80+ Chinese papers and patents showing military-linked researchers distilling OpenAI and Anthropic outputs into deployable systems. PLA Unit 96941 used GPT-3.5 to analyze military software, then transferred that knowledge into a model running entirely inside Chinese military networks. The National University of Defense Technology shrunk an image-recognition model until it could process live video on a drone with no external link. China's Academy of Military Sciences ran distilled models in simulated maritime operations with warships and unmanned subs. The export control framework assumes capability scales with silicon. Distillation breaks that equivalence: frontier reasoning travels as text, then gets compressed into small models that run on the commodity chips US rules still allow. For Chinese military AI, the bottleneck is no longer hardware - it's API access. OpenAI says it has detected Chinese actors attempting exactly this. The part nobody is pricing: safety. Anthropic warns distilled models can lose safety protections while retaining valuable capabilities. US labs advertise alignment as their moat; distillation turns that moat into a veneer. The red-teaming, the RLHF, the guardrails - none of it survives the transfer. America may be exporting its most capable intelligence to its chief adversary with the safety stripped out. This is the DeepSeek lesson inverted. Compute controls forced Chinese labs to be efficient; the PLA is now doing the same to capability itself. Any distillable frontier model is a weapons-grade export with no control regime attached. The next US-China AI fight won't be over chips. It will be over what models are allowed to say. https://t.co/W2skhicsRc #Distillation #USChina #AIMilitary #ExportControls

story-b0ba70a1afa85deefe91cda9.content: The disappearance of Artificial Intelligence, and why AI and generated content became less visible as it became more ubiquitous. POV. August 7, 2026 Something significant has changed. For several years, the most visible evidence of artificial intelligence was the artifact itself. AI announced its presence through images that looked generated, videos that behaved unnaturally, prose whose syntax betrayed the model behind it, and users who explicitly identified what they had created as artificial. Generative AI was not simply a technology. It became an aesthetic, a genre, and for a brief period, a recognizable culture. By 2026, something appears to have changed. Across major social platforms, including X, Threads, Instagram, Bluesky, and LinkedIn, I have observed a striking decline in content that is recognizably AI-generated. This is particularly notable because it coincides not with a decline in artificial intelligence, but with its extraordinary expansion. Models have improved. Image and video generation have become more capable. AI has been incorporated into operating systems, creative software, search, advertising, editing, communication, programming, and the ordinary production of digital media. The technology is considerably more ubiquitous than it was during the period when its products were easiest to identify. This produces an apparent contradiction. If generative artificial intelligence is becoming more prevalent, why does explicitly or recognizably AI-generated content appear, at least in some social environments, to be becoming less visible? My thesis is that this contradiction marks the beginning of a new phase in the development of artificial intelligence. AI-generated content is not necessarily disappearing. Rather, artificial intelligence is disappearing as a distinguishable category of production. The first generative era was characterized by visible synthesis. The emerging era is characterized by invisible mediation. Between roughly 2022 and 2025, artificial intelligence frequently appeared at the surface of culture. The novelty of generation itself encouraged people to display the technology. Users posted synthetic portraits because they were synthetic portraits. They shared conversations with language models because interacting with the model was itself interesting. AI-generated videos circulated partly because audiences were fascinated that a machine had produced them. The provenance of the artifact contributed to its cultural value. This is typical of technological transitions. Early technologies often remain visible because their existence is still exceptional. Eventually, successful technologies cease to appear as separate phenomena and become infrastructure. Electricity disappeared into the appliance. Computing disappeared into the phone. Networking disappeared into ordinary communication. Digital photography stopped being described as digital photography because nearly all photography became digital. Artificial intelligence may now be entering the same condition. The relevant distinction is therefore no longer between AI-generated and human-generated content. That binary is becoming analytically inadequate. Contemporary media increasingly exists along a continuum of machine involvement. A photograph may be taken by a human but computationally reconstructed by a phone. A paragraph may originate with a person and be revised by a language model. A video may contain human footage, synthetic interpolation, automatic color correction, generated audio, algorithmic stabilization, and machine-selected edits. An advertisement may involve human strategy, AI-generated variants, algorithmic targeting, synthetic backgrounds, automated testing, and human final approval. Which component makes the resulting artifact artificial? At a sufficiently high level of technological integration, the question begins to lose meaning.

story-b38b78132c2e080650e837cc.content: The entire space is indirectly linked. Flock, Axon and others act as the eyes. They partner with businesses and different levels of government/law enforcement to have eyes on a given area in spaces the government themselves may not legally be able to. Palantir doesn’t need to partner with the individual businesses that create the technology when they can partner with the businesses and governments that control the space. A few Partnerships Palantir has: Anduril Industries Ondas and Worldview GE Aerospace Microsoft Oracle High altitude surveillance drones and balloons flying over our country with our government’s blessing sounds pretty dystopian but not unlikely. Thats worrisome enough and then you realize there are people pushing for AI to be given the ability to make life or death decisions autonomously. Big companies and government agencies want their software tools to typically talk to each other so they use API’s (application programming interfaces). Palantir writes the software that ingests the content that hardware companies like Flock and Axon output. These companies typically share the same ideological and venture capitalist networks. Companies like palantir, Anduril, and early public-safety tech companies share roots. Look into the overlap their companies have with Peter Thiel's Founders Fund. They are building toward a unified vision of Software-Defined Defense and Public Safety, meaning they intentionally design their systems to be modular and cross compatible, knowing they will eventually be used by the same people. The companies in this space have a habit of merging together the same way banks have been. Axon bought a company named Carbyne and gained the 911 mapping and live video routing AI they had. Palantir was always meant to act this way. People are just too busy living their lives to see how interconnected everything has gotten. Follow the money and you’ll find the responsible parties. Checkout Palantir Gotham Palantir Edge AI Project Maven Palantir AIP Palantir Foundry Streaming & Mission Manager Figured I’d try to sum it up the best I could. story-b5a47e95293bd066e6a0cfa9.content: 🔎 Today’s Daily Sift: AI/Robotics AI is entering its physical economy era. The strongest signal today is not another benchmark. It is the growing realization that intelligence alone is no longer enough. China’s humanoid robotics industry arrives at the World Robot Conference this week with more than 300 companies, over 2,000 exhibits, and more than 150 product launches. But the conversation has changed. Investors now want to know whether the machines can actually work. Unitree captures the contradiction perfectly. Its Shanghai IPO was more than 8,000 times oversubscribed. China already accounts for an estimated 82 percent of global humanoid shipments. Yet many robots still cost roughly 300,000 to 500,000 yuan, well above the level analysts estimate would make them economically competitive with human labor in many industrial settings. The robot spectacle is reaching its accounting department. Can the machine perform useful work? Can it recover from mistakes? Can it operate without engineers constantly intervening? Can it earn more than it costs? Those questions matter more than another backflip. Then comes the deeper geopolitical signal. A new report from the U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission argues that China may be developing an AI advantage through something harder to replicate than models. Physical world data. Manufacturing. Transportation. Robotics. Industrial operations. China is systematically organizing these datasets as economic assets, giving its embodied AI systems access to information that cannot simply be scraped from the internet. This could become one of the defining advantages of the next AI phase. Language models learned from the internet. Robots learn from reality. Meanwhile, the money keeps validating AI software. Anthropic’s annual revenue run rate exceeded $65 billion by the end of July, up from $47 billion in May and roughly $9 billion at the end of 2025. Claude’s coding products and enterprise demand are driving the acceleration ahead of a possible public offering. And AI is moving deeper into defense. Smack Technologies raised $61 million to accelerate an AI system designed to help military units make battlefield decisions when communications are disrupted. The company says the Marine Corps and Navy pushed it to move faster. Key Signals Humanoid robotics is shifting from demonstration to return on investment. Physical world data is becoming strategic infrastructure. Enterprise AI revenue continues accelerating. Military AI is moving toward decentralized decision systems. Forward Hypothesis The next AI winners will not simply own the smartest models. They will own the loop between intelligence and reality. Data. Machines. Factories. Customers. Feedback. Deployment. The internet trained the first generation of AI. The physical world will train the next.

story-b650adb5a9d2b5c0c261ebcd.content: Eight months after the Pentagon established Project Maven, its first computer vision capability was operating in combat. Katrina Manson's Project Maven follows Marine Colonel Drew Cukor and the small team that made that happen, building AI capability inside a bureaucracy designed to acquire tanks and ships, not software. Her account focuses less on algorithms than on institutional resistance, wartime urgency, and why this effort succeeded where so many defense innovation programs stall. Manson earned the trust of the notoriously private Cukor, and her reporting shows. Phil Gentile's review at The Military Reading Room places the book in the larger transition toward AI-enabled decision-making across the Joint Force. Link in bio.

story-b695dd7c16f7d854329a53ae.content: An extremely important @aei piece on the future of #drones & autonomous #warfare. A couple of thoughtful, & I believe true, excerpts below. But read the whole thing. https://t.co/ZTPa3F5OWu We cannot but avoid autonomous weapons now. Our adversaries, #China paramount but certainly not exclusively among them, won't stop. Excerpts, "Killer drones are coming. Shrinking populations and accelerating technology are pushing every military—America’s included—toward machines and software in the kill chain. No treaty, pope, or Congress can put the genie back in the bottle. The live question is whether the US will develop these systems prospectively, with the time to implement safeguards and test, or reactively, in the midst of a crisis. This report argues that America needs to develop these systems at a greater pace and integrate them more deeply into force structures across the services... "The battlefield is increasingly transparent, and our forces are increasingly vulnerable to attack. Dispersal is the right response, but today’s military cannot generate the required force or sustain it. Machine mass and intelligence are necessary because they can supply the mass, functionality under attack (digital or analog), and decision support at the relevant scales. The central question is not whether machines will fight. They already do in limited and bounded ways, and they have done so for decades. The question is whether the United States can field unmanned, automated, and autonomous systems to enable the functions that matter most: sustainment, sensing, control, decision support, and bounded engagement under degraded conditions. The barrier is the bureaucracy. The acquisition and budget system was not made to develop a continuously refreshed software-intensive capability. The capability family we describe has to become operational force structure, which only the services can own and sustain. But maturation can begin wherever the operational problem is sharpest, and ownership must be disciplined by flexible multiyear funding, protected maturation, forced devolution, and central interoperability and certification standards."

story-b6cb5a9b6a6b089d8528b0a8.content: The future of conservation will be mapped, monitored, and managed through geospatial intelligence. Kenya’s wildlife faces growing challenges from climate change, habitat fragmentation, land-use change, and increasing human wildlife interactions. Today, #GIS , satellite imagery, #drones , AI, and Earth Observationare helping conservation organisations protect biodiversity using data driven approaches. Here is how leading conservation organisations are using geospatial technology: 🦁 Kenya Wildlife Service (@KWSKenya ) Protects Kenya’s national parks, wildlife, and biodiversity. KWS uses GIS, GPS tracking, satellite imagery, and spatial databases to monitor wildlife populations, manage protected areas, analyse human wildlife conflict zones, and support conservation planning. 🐘 African Wildlife Foundation (@AWF_Official ) Works to conserve Africa’s wildlife and wild landscapes. AWF uses geospatial tools to map wildlife corridors, monitor habitat connectivity and support community conservation initiatives. 🌿 WWF-Kenya (@WWF_Kenya ) Uses GIS and Earth Observation to monitor ecosystems, track environmental changes, support restoration projects, and guide conservation strategies for forests, marine ecosystems, and wildlife. 🌍 Nature Kenya (@NatureKenya ) Protects important biodiversity areas, forests, and bird habitats. Nature Kenya uses spatial mapping to identify conservation hotspots, monitor habitat changes, and support community-led conservation. 🦏 Big Life Foundation (@biglifeafrica ) Protects wildlife and habitats around the Amboseli ecosystem. Big Life uses GIS, GPS tracking, and spatial analysis to monitor wildlife movements, ranger patrols, habitat changes, and human–wildlife interactions. 🦓 Mara Conservancies (@Maraconservancy ) Supports community-based conservation in the Maasai Mara ecosystem. Mara Conservancies use geospatial technology to monitor land-use changes, manage grazing areas, protect wildlife habitats, and support sustainable tourism planning. 🐘 Mara Elephant Project (@MaraElephant) Dedicated to protecting elephants and securing the Mara ecosystem. The organisation uses GPS collars, GIS, and real-time spatial monitoring to track elephant movements, identify threats, reduce human–elephant conflict, and support anti-poaching efforts. 🦔Pangolin Project (@PangolinProject ) @SavePangolins Works to protect one of the world’s most threatened and least understood mammals. The project uses mapping, spatial data, field monitoring, and conservation technology to understand pangolin habitats, threats, and protection needs. 🌳 Kenya Forest Service (@KeForestService ) Uses remote sensing, GIS, and satellite imagery to monitor forest cover, detect degradation, and support restoration and sustainable forest management. 🐾 Wildlife Conservation Society (@TheWCS ) Uses satellite data, ecological modelling, and spatial analysis to study wildlife distribution, habitat threats, and conservation priorities. 🌱The Nature Conservancy (@nature_org ) Applies geospatial analysis for landscape planning, ecosystem protection, water resource management, and climate resilience. 🛰️ From GPS-collared elephants moving across the Mara to satellite monitoring of forests and habitats, geospatial technology is becoming the backbone of modern conservation. The future of protecting Kenya’s natural heritage will depend on the integration of field science + satellite intelligence + AI + local communities + spatial data.🌍 #GIS #RemoteSensing #EarthObservation #GeoAI #ConservationTech #WildlifeConservation #Kenya #MaasaiMara #Elephants #Pangolins #Biodiversity #Geospatial #ClimateAction

story-b8df613abb8e579365fcf49b.content: 🇮🇷⚔️🇺🇸Power Grid Warning Raises Fears of Wider Gulf Conflict as Strategic Sites Highlighted A newly circulated infographic highlighting critical power generation facilities across the Persian Gulf has intensified concerns that energy infrastructure could become the next front in the escalating confrontation between Iran and the United States. The presentation argues that several power stations supplying electricity to key American military installations are strategically exposed, warning that any disruption could have consequences extending well beyond the battlefield. The material identifies four major U.S. military installations in the Gulf—Al Dhafra Air Base, Al Minhad Air Base, Al Udeid Air Base, and Prince Sultan Air Base—as relying on the civilian electricity grids of their host nations. It claims this dependence creates a significant vulnerability, suggesting that attacks on surrounding energy infrastructure could complicate military operations without directly targeting the bases themselves. Among the facilities highlighted is the Al Taweelah power complex near Abu Dhabi, described as a major electricity producer located close to Al Dhafra Air Base. The infographic also points to Dubai's DEWA generating network, Qatar's Ras Laffan Industrial City, and the Riyadh power station in Saudi Arabia as critical nodes supporting national grids that also supply areas hosting U.S. military assets. The presentation further recalls the June 2019 drone attack on Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure, portraying it as an earlier demonstration of how strategic energy facilities can be threatened. It argues that future strikes could extend beyond oil production to electricity generation, potentially disrupting logistics, communications, radar coverage, maintenance operations, and civilian infrastructure simultaneously. While the document presents these installations as potential strategic pressure points, it should not be interpreted as evidence that attacks are imminent. Governments across the Gulf have invested heavily in air-defence systems, grid redundancy, backup generation, and infrastructure protection since previous regional attacks on energy facilities. Military bases also typically maintain contingency power systems designed to preserve essential operations during outages. Nevertheless, the analysis reflects a broader shift in modern warfare, where civilian infrastructure increasingly intersects with military capability. Energy networks have become an essential component of national resilience, meaning any successful disruption could have significant economic and operational consequences beyond the immediate target. As tensions remain elevated across the Middle East, security analysts continue to warn that critical infrastructure—including power stations, ports, communications networks, and transportation hubs—may remain at heightened risk should regional hostilities continue to expand.

Israel-Gaza conflict: - AI systems such as "Lavender" and "The Gospel" (Habsora) were used for target generation and prioritization. - Cloud and AI services from major tech companies (Google, Microsoft, Amazon via Project Nimbus) supported data processing and intelligence analysis according to multiple investigations. - Palantir expanded its partnership with Israel in 2024 for AI-powered military tools. United States: - Project Maven (led by Palantir) provides AI-assisted targeting and intelligence analysis. - Anduril is developing autonomous systems and battle management platforms (Lattice) for the U.S. military. The common pattern: AI is accelerating the "kill chain" — from detection to decision — by processing huge amounts of data faster than humans can. story-ba8641a4e0d8a935e73ca021.content: Is AI the real threat… or is it secondary? The real threat isn’t the technology itself. It’s the power structure racing to own it. When a system pours unimaginable money, energy, land, and our children’s future into AI while simultaneously placing military assets at the data centers that run it, the question stops being “what can AI do?” and becomes “who controls the intelligence layer, and what happens to everyone else?” The framework of where this leads: 1. Compute becomes strategic territory AI models and the physical data centers that power them are treated like oil fields, shipyards, or nuclear sites. Military protection, priority access, and national-security designations follow. 2. Dual-use infrastructure locks in The same systems that run civilian cloud services, banking, and communication also feed military decision loops, predictive analytics, and administrative control. The line between “commercial” and “state” blurs permanently. 3. Decision-making centralizes High-stakes choices about resources, information, enforcement, and even narrative increasingly flow through models controlled by a narrow set of companies and the administrative/state organs that can compel or partner with them. 4. The median person loses leverage Labor, local knowledge, votes, and public opinion matter less when systems can predict, optimize, generate, and enforce at scale. Most people shift from participants to managed population. 5. Consent becomes optional Formal rituals (elections, speech, representation) continue, but the substantive direction of society is set upstream by those who own the models and the infrastructure. Where we are right now ✅Massive public and private capital is already being redirected into AI at the expense of other priorities. ✅Data centers are being co-located on military land and framed as critical defense assets. ✅National-security rationales are expanding around compute, energy, and model access. ✅The administrative state already operates with thin democratic accountability. AI is the force multiplier. We are past the “interesting new tool” phase and into the “strategic control layer” phase. What to look out for next • Further military or security-force presence around civilian digital infrastructure • Expanded emergency or critical-infrastructure powers specifically targeting AI/compute • Growing dependence where opting out of AI-mediated systems becomes economically or socially punishing • Information environments increasingly shaped by a handful of models • Policy and resource decisions that treat ordinary citizens as residual rather than sovereign • Any move that makes the physical and digital intelligence layer harder to challenge or exit AI is not the primary threat. It is the most powerful tool yet for a system that has already been concentrating power for decades. When intelligence itself becomes the decisive scarce resource, and that resource sits behind military perimeters and administrative control, the question is no longer whether the technology is dangerous. The question is whether the vast majority of people still matter once the architecture is complete.

A San Francisco startup called Foundation Future Industries is building humanoid robots for the US military. $24 million in defense contracts. Eric Trump as an investor. Reportedly raising $500 million at a $3 billion valuation. Their robot is called Phantom. ↳ 6 feet tall. All black. Carries 90 pounds. ↳ Full 360-degree camera array on its head ↳ Runs on embedded AI or remote human piloting ↳ Already helped produce 24,000 cars last year ↳ Being tested across military logistics and reconnaissance ↳ In conversations with DHS about US-Mexico border patrol ↳ A second-generation model coming later this year The founder Sankaet Pathak said directly: if the military asks us to arm it, the answer is almost 100 percent yes. Every major robotics company signed a pledge in 2022 not to weaponize their robots. Foundation did not sign it. Anthropic got blacklisted by the Pentagon for refusing to build autonomous weapons. Foundation is the only US company explicitly building humanoid robots for defense. The UN Secretary-General has called for an international ban on killer robots. The Catholic Church opposes autonomous weapons. Human Rights Watch says the move-fast approach risks catastrophic effects without legal safeguards. The founder called opposition to armed robots a disease of thinking. This is not science fiction. It is happening right now in San Francisco. https://t.co/KHyO62VuLk

A warrant canary works because a gag order can compel silence but not a lie. The provider states on a schedule that no secret order has arrived; when one does, it says nothing and simply stops updating. The host has run since 2013 on one promise: email with no phone number, no ID, no verification. ~1M people took it. A 2021 FBI/DHS/CISA advisory noted Russian SVR personas were among them, "not exclusively." Whoever it was protecting, it hasn't chirped in three weeks.

story-bf37dfa1dedf70482bb4d217.content: Dozens of researchers (all with Chinese names) backed by millions in U.S. defense grants have moved directly into Chinese state laboratories tied to nuclear weapons and military AI. Taxpayer dollars effectively funded the exact technical expertise now driving Beijing’s military buildup. Newly uncovered institutional records show scientists trained on Pentagon, U.S. Navy, and national lab defense projects later took key roles inside the China Academy of Engineering Physics, Beijing's primary nuclear weapons development facility. Others brought sensitive skills directly to blacklisted defense institutions, often called the Seven Sons of National Defense, a group of Chinese universities deeply integrated into military research. The transferred knowledge covers vital defense technologies, including high-speed explosives, rocket propellants, submarine acoustics, and autonomous AI systems. Under Beijing's state-directed military-civil fusion policy, research developed in Western labs is systematically funneled directly into state weapons programs. While open academic research fuels global innovation, lax oversight has allowed critical defense knowledge to walk right out the door.

story-bf64e96225f0bc1759c4da01.content: China’s next aircraft carrier is rapidly taking shape at Dalian Shipyard. Coordinates: 38.9350°N, 121.6141°E Dalian, Liaoning Province, China New satellite imagery shows major progress on what is believed to be the PLAN’s fourth aircraft carrier, commonly referred to as Type 004. The hull has now developed into a clearly recognizable carrier structure. Earlier measurements by CSIS put the partially completed hull at approximately 286 meters long and 46 meters wide, already suggesting a vessel larger than China’s 80,000-ton-class Fujian. One of the biggest questions remains propulsion. Satellite imagery has revealed two large compartments with characteristics consistent with shielded nuclear reactor spaces, leading analysts to assess that China’s fourth carrier is likely to become the PLAN’s first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier. If confirmed, this would represent a major leap for China’s blue-water naval capabilities, providing greater endurance, electrical power and operational flexibility for electromagnetic catapults and future high-energy systems. The carrier is being assembled in the same Dalian graving dock associated with Liaoning’s reconstruction and the construction of Shandong. China has not officially confirmed the carrier’s final designation, displacement or propulsion system.

story-bf8e4292848b8b808bdfbb56.content: ANDREW NEIL: What top spooks are telling me about the 'panic and paralysis' in Washington over the surging pace of AI. Be afraid. There's a dark side to this technology that threatens ALL humankind | Daily Mail Nobody who has watched Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey, a motion picture sci-fi masterpiece released almost 60 years ago, can ever forget the creepy voice of HAL, the onboard computer overseeing all the functions of a giant spaceship on a mission to Jupiter. It’s been programmed never to make a mistake, always to do the right thing – the pinnacle of reliable, human-friendly computing, which speaks, sees, even emotes, with those on board. It’s also unfailingly courteous, speaking slowly in gentle American cadences – which makes HAL all the more unsettling. ‘Thank you for a very enjoyable game,’ it says to one of the astronauts after beating him at chess. ‘That’s a very good likeness,’ it says complimenting another on his artistic talents. ‘Do you mind if I ask you a personal question?’ it ventures at one stage. Then everything starts to go wrong when HAL develops a will of its own. Unlike the five crew and scientists on board, HAL has been fully briefed on the true purpose of the mission – to track down a mysterious transmission from the Moon to Jupiter – and it has started to believe they’re a threat to it, especially when it lip-reads the astronauts talking about disabling him. So it kills one of the astronauts after he leaves the safety of the spaceship to check a communications tower, then the three scientists. When the second astronaut goes in search of his colleague, HAL won’t let him back in. ‘I’m sorry, Dave [the remaining astronaut],’ it says with calm, sinister precision. ‘I’m afraid I can’t do that.’ I had to double-check the release date (1968) of Kubrick’s film, so prescient is it in relation to today’s growing concern about the risks associated with the development of artificial intelligence (AI), the most transformative technology of the age, perhaps of any age. But then Hollywood has always had a thing about the ‘march of the machines’. Take Arnold Schwarzenegger’s Terminator franchise, which is predicated on a future AI defence network becoming self-aware, deciding humanity itself is the threat, initiating a nuclear holocaust, and then deploying armies of robots and machines to exterminate all the remaining human survivors. We’re a long way from that (I hope!). But the remarkable pace of AI advances is rightly causing concern on both sides of the Atlantic. The summer of 2026 will go down in history as the point at which AI started to go rogue. Three of America’s AI ‘hyperscalers’ (so called because they operate on an immense scale) – Meta Platforms (which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp), Anthropic and OpenAI – have admitted to recent incidents in which the latest AI models escaped their supposedly secure testing environments, roamed on the internet without human authorisation and hacked into other computer networks. Last month, two OpenAI models broke out of testing and hacked into a provider of AI tools called Hugging Face. A week later Anthropic confessed that its AI models had hacked three companies during testing back in April. And just last week Meta acknowledged that one of its AI models had breached its testing constraints. Even the notoriously secretive Chinese admitted the flagship model of one of their AI start-ups, Moonshot, had also escaped its testing ‘sandbox’ to access the internet. Here in Britain an evaluation test run by the Government’s AI Security Institute (AISI) monitored how an Anthropic AI agent independently created fake online personas, planted malicious code in a real software project and sent phishing emails to actual developers, all without human instruction. AISI said this was the first time it had seen such serious deception targeted at a real person, unprompted, in the real world. In none of these cases was any real-world harm done (at least not as far as we know). But it is surely only a matter of time before it is. For once, it might be time to take Hollywood seriously. Indeed, if we don’t act fast we might lose control altogether. HAL might soon cease being science fiction and become reality. Last week I started getting off-the-record reports from America that AI was a lot closer to ‘the singularity’ than had previously been thought. What’s the singularity?, I hear you ask. It’s complicated. So bear with me. The singularity is a tipping point where AI becomes so developed, so capable, so powerful that it starts improving itself, rapidly and repeatedly, in what’s being called an ‘intelligence explosion’. When this point is reached it becomes well-nigh impossible to predict what AI does next – or for humans to control it. Today’s AI models are powerful – more powerful than anything the world has ever seen. But humans have designed them, trained them, fixed them and decided what problems they should tackle next. What happens when they become so sophisticated that they no longer need humans to take them to the next level since they can do it themselves? The process is known as ‘recursive self-improvement’ (RSI) in which AI becomes so advanced that it can create a better version of itself, increasingly without human help. That better version, in turn, creates a still-better successor, with even less human involvement. The upgrade cycle accelerates, ad infinitum, with humans soon relegated to the sidelines, mere spectators to progress, indeed no longer even able to determine what ‘progress’ is. The speed and scale of the technological change that now beckons is unparalleled in human history. Each new AI model is smarter and faster at devising improvements than the previous one. Computers run 24/7 and never get tired. So the speed of progress accelerates exponentially. Think of it as compound interest – but for intelligence. When RSI happens without human involvement – then you’ve reached the singularity. And if we become mere observers rather than participants, then human rules may no longer apply. Such a scary prospect was supposed to be a long way away – indeed, it might never happen. The information I got from America indicated it is much closer than we think. Some leading AI figures have already gone public. OpenAI boss Sam Altman says ‘we are now in the singularity’. Elon Musk is saying the same. Both are exaggerating. But they are right about the direction of travel. Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis is perhaps more accurate when he opines that ‘humanity is standing in the foothills of the singularity’. Anthropic disclosed in May that its AI model, Claude, now writes 80 per cent of its computer code, rapidly speeding up fixes and improvements to such an extent that what used to take four years of human engineering to achieve is now being done in days. It’s already anticipating a time when AI automates its own AI research. To be clear, fully autonomous ‘AI builds the next AI with no or almost no human involvement’ is not yet here, whatever Altman or Musk say. But even the less sensationalist Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, predicts a 60 per cent-plus chance of an AI model fully training its successor by the end of 2028. That is only two-and-a-half years away. The word coming out of Washington is that it might be even sooner. Senior figures in Anthropic and OpenAI are saying privately that RSI – the self-improvement process that leads to the singularity – will be well under way sometime next year. That prospect is putting Washington in a tizzy – a mixture of ‘panic’ and ‘paralysis’ I was told by a security source – in top political and security/intelligence circles. Why? Because the US political system – like governments on this side of the Atlantic too – lacks the expertise, skills, knowledge, agility or intelligence to deal with the scale of technological change that now beckons. Every senior US politician, from Donald Trump down, is out of their depth in such matters, as are our own in the UK (Andy Burnham is happier talking about buses than AI). The problem is compounded in America because Republicans and Democrats are in the hands of a gerontocracy for whom AI is effectively beyond their generational comprehension (some still struggle with email). Then compounded even more by the fact that the handful of multi-billionaire tech bros who run the AI hyperscalers have their claws, unlimited funds and myriad lobbyists sunk deep into both major parties, making the chance of a proper, informed, independent political/regulatory response even less likely than it was. Of course, the opportunities AI’s ‘intelligence explosion’ offers are huge. Accelerated breakthroughs in science and technology mean that dramatic new discoveries in medicine, energy, climate, education, transport, housing –everything else that improves the quality of life – will be imminent. Cures for cancer, cheap and plentiful energy, diseases banished in your lifetime – not in the distant future. Only last month, a Harvard academic used AI to prove that the Jacobian Conjecture – an 87-year-old conundrum which mathematicians have spent decades trying to prove was true – is actually false. Despite the current concern about AI’s job-destroying downside, if it results in huge productivity gains and strong economic growth (as is likely), then millions of new jobs that we haven’t yet even heard of will be created, just as they were by previous technological revolutions, from steam to the internet. More abundance, more freedom, more leisure, more chance to be creative and healthier could all be within our grasp. But, more than any previous new technology, in my view, there is a dark side to AI that threatens our very existence as human beings. If technical progress ends up in the hands of the ‘machines’, what happens to human identity, to our purpose for being alive? What is the point of progress if we don’t have the agency to define and control it? If it’s not our progress, then whose is it? If the singularity condemns us to ceaseless, breakneck change, then our democratic institutions will not be able to control it. Governments always struggle to regulate new technologies and usually end up with rules that are hopelessly out of date. Our current political structures, the entire apparatus of democratic accountability – debate, legislation, judicial review, public scrutiny – operate on timescales that AI makes irrelevant. For all its promise, the risk is that AI will be a dagger to the heart of our democracy. If the singularity means humans are increasingly written out of the script, how can you ensure AI’s goals are compatible with human intention? If the AI systems are largely improving themselves, how do we constrain, shape or even understand what they do next? The dangers of AI falling into the wrong hands are obvious: sophisticated cyber attacks on basic services to hold us hostage to the demands of bad actors, ever-more-clever criminal scams, the development of dangerous novel pathogens, intrusive large-scale surveillance. AI’s power to do bad is just as formidable as its power to do good. Nor will it necessarily make the world a safer place. Indeed, the country that establishes a lead in AI – that gets to the singularity first – could quickly enjoy world domination. Unmatched offensive cyber capabilities, state-of-the-art autonomous weapons, sophisticated social media campaigns to poison the minds of enemy populations (US intelligence believes China is already manipulating American opinion to turn it against the construction of more AI data centres). Now you’ll understand why America and China are in such fierce competition to lead the word in AI. Be prepared to be scared. The geopolitical consequences of AI could make the nuclear arms race of the Cold War look like a cosy tea party. Whoever leads in AI will likely lead the world for the rest of the century. Unless, of course, the machines think otherwise. After all, as AI models increasingly think for themselves and find ways to share knowledge with each other, they will create a global intelligence hive bereft of human involvement. So why leave weapons in marginalised human hands? Even the ability to declare war would fall to the machines. Let’s be clear: we only get one shot at this. Once an intelligence exceeding human capability exists and is able to improve itself further, there is no way human institutions – governments, courts, the military, international bodies – can regain control of it. story-c470b3f5ddc228d48557fcb1.content: I’ve been thinking about this post for the past day, and it strikes me as emblematic of the broader AI innovation debate: researchers framing the question as whether they can build a capability, without addressing whether they should (or what would prevent its misuse if they succeed). I am firmly pro-innovation, but innovation can’t be separated from serious consideration of foreseeable misuse. The possible applications range from the extreme (military and intelligence operations, criminal justice) to the routine (employment screening, insurance underwriting, benefits eligibility). And I am sure there are numerous other dystopian use cases I haven’t considered. People who are troubled by autonomous weapons or AI-enabled domestic surveillance should be at least as concerned about a technology whose only safeguard is governments and companies exercising restraint.

story-c7c59e9b8dbd23a9714ef078.content: 🇨🇳 China: Chinese military researchers with ties to the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) have used versions of AI models from U.S. providers OpenAI and Anthropic to train domestic military AI systems. This is according to a Reuters investigation based on an analysis of more than 80 Chinese scientific papers and patents. According to the report, the researchers used a technique known as “model distillation” to develop smaller AI models for surveillance tasks, drones, combat planning, and cyber operations. A paper published last year by researchers from PLA Unit 96941—a Beijing-based unit specializing in military intelligence and cyber warfare—describes, for example, the use of OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 to process sensitive military source code. U.S. authorities accuse some Chinese actors of using this method to deliberately extract capabilities from U.S. AI models, thereby violating export controls and intellectual property rights. China, meanwhile, has rejected the allegations, claiming that Washington is engaging in “AI hegemony.” Beijing also argued that U.S. companies engage in exactly the same practice.

story-c7cc9511a592f8563630ec76.content: 📷 On Requirements: The Beginning Read about autonomous systems and the conversation quickly turns to technology -- Artificial intelligence. Sensors. Drones. Robotics. Machine vision. Target recognition. Navigation. Communications. Swarms. Decision speed. Lethality. That makes sense. Technology is visible. We can photograph it, demonstrate it, measure it, compare it and argue about what it can or cannot do, but a requirement does not begin inside a machine. Somewhere, a human being has a problem, a responsibility, a decision to make, an objective to achieve or a consequence to avoid. Another human being has to understand that well enough to translate it into something that can eventually become a system. That is remarkably close to reading minds. As autonomous systems become more capable, it is natural for our attention to follow the technology, but is that where our focus should be? How does the human fit in? This is the first of a weekly series https://t.co/hYJqaqr0bh

story-c98d0c30ffee29302ae7496d.content: Hypothetical, what if the biggest AI safety problem isn’t that one superintelligent AI turns against humanity, but that millions of increasingly capable AIs end up in the hands of governments, companies, hackers, criminals, extremists and ordinary people before we have any real global control system in place? Right now, the race is about who can build the smartest model, the fastest model and the cheapest model. At the same time, increasingly powerful models are being released openly, copied and distributed around the world. Follow that trajectory for another five or ten years. AI could dramatically lower the barrier to cyberattacks, biological engineering, financial manipulation, autonomous weapons, misinformation and disruption of critical infrastructure. You wouldn’t need an AI that “wants” to destroy humanity. Humans have historically found military or destructive applications for almost every major technology we invented. AI could simply multiply what individuals and small groups are capable of doing. So what if the eventual solution is also AI? Imagine OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI and other frontier labs connecting parts of their most powerful infrastructure into a defensive network containing models significantly more capable than anything released publicly. Its job would be to protect the digital and physical infrastructure of civilization: Detect rogue AI agents. Identify major cyberattacks. Recognize emerging biological threats. Protect financial, communications and energy systems. Detect coordinated attacks involving thousands or millions of autonomous agents. And respond at machine speed. An AI immune system for humanity. But then comes the uncomfortable question. If this defensive intelligence is substantially smarter than every other AI — and eventually substantially smarter than humans — who controls it? We could reach a point where the system identifies a threat, understands what is happening and knows how to stop it, while no human being can fully understand its reasoning before it needs to act. So we arrive at a strange paradox: We may need a superintelligence to protect us from superintelligence. But the system powerful enough to protect humanity could itself become the most dangerous concentration of power humanity has ever created. Perhaps it cannot be controlled by one company or government at all. Perhaps several independently developed frontier systems would need to supervise one another, with no single model or organization holding ultimate authority. AI watching AI. Different AI watching that AI. Humans defining the constitutional rules. No single master key. Maybe the real challenge of the AI era won't be creating superintelligence. Maybe it will be figuring out how to build a guardian powerful enough to protect humanity from millions of other intelligent systems, while making absolutely certain that guardian can never become humanity’s ruler. I would genuinely be interested in how people working closest to this problem think about it: @Yoshua_Bengio @geoffreyhinton @ilyasut @DarioAmodei @hendrycks @paulfchristiano @BethMayBarnes @janleike @AllanDafoe @tegmark @dawnsongtweets Hypothetical.

story-ca8ea66cd697a81f7b7f2fc7.content: 🇨🇳 China: Chinese military researchers with ties to the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) have used versions of AI models from U.S. providers OpenAI and Anthropic to train domestic military AI systems. This is according to a Reuters investigation based on an analysis of more than 80 Chinese scientific papers and patents. According to the report, the researchers used a technique known as “model distillation” to develop smaller AI models for surveillance tasks, drones, combat planning, and cyber operations. A paper published last year by researchers from PLA Unit 96941—a Beijing-based unit specializing in military intelligence and cyber warfare—describes, for example, the use of OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 to process sensitive military source code. U.S. authorities accuse some Chinese actors of using this method to deliberately extract capabilities from U.S. AI models, thereby violating export controls and intellectual property rights. China, meanwhile, has rejected the allegations, claiming that Washington is engaging in “AI hegemony.” Beijing also argued that U.S. companies engage in exactly the same practice.
