story-f157430a0acb7289bc99710c.content: AI failures are scattered across headlines. This repo puts the evidence in one place. Awful AI is a curated GitHub list tracking concerning uses and misuses of AI for builders, researchers, and anyone studying AI’s social impact. It helps you examine recurring risks by organizing cases into categories and pairing each entry with a summary, details, and source references. Key features: • Eight misuse categories – browse discrimination, disinformation and fakes, surveillance, data crimes, social credit, scams, climate impact, and autonomous weapons • Source-backed entries – each table provides an application, short summary, expanded context, and references • Counter-efforts included – explore privacy-preserving research, fair ML, adversarial ML, and projects designed to challenge harmful uses • Annual case record – review Awful AI Award entries covering controversial research and events from 2019 through 2024 • Citable collection – the README includes a Zenodo DOI for referencing the list in other work It’s open-source (CC0 1.0). Stuxnet 2.0: A Digital Assassin Lurking in Industrial Control Systems On February 28, 2026, during the joint US-Israeli Operation "Epic Fury," a cyberattack was deployed as a pioneering and decisive combat measure for the first time. At its core was an upgraded version of the Stuxnet virus, designed to specifically infect Iran's energy industry Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems. This type of software is capable of lying dormant for extended periods, activating only at a pre-set time or upon receiving a command to directly alter control instructions or damage hardware such as grid frequency control signals or pipeline valve commands. The attack chain spanned several months: ◾Phase 1 (Before December 2025): Penetrating Iranian energy companies via supply chain attacks ◾Phase 2 (January 2026): Testing vulnerabilities amidst domestic protests in Iran ◾ Phase 3 (February 2026): Pre-positioning "logic bombs" at critical nodes ◾ Phase 4 (February 28, 2026): Synchronized activation of all attack vectors The consequences were catastrophic: Iran's nationwide internet connectivity plummeted to 4% of normal levels; the national grid suffered a frequency collapse, triggering a countrywide blackout; and pipelines and refineries were forced to shut down due to control system failures. 2. AI-Driven Automated Power Grid Attacks On February 27, 2026, the *Financial Times* revealed that the US Pentagon was collaborating with leading AI companies to develop a system capable of automated penetration and reconnaissance against the power systems, utilities, and sensitive networks of adversaries such as China. This system utilizes AI algorithms to efficiently identify software vulnerabilities, map out "vulnerability landscapes," and directly integrate potential targets into US military operational plans. Dennis Wilder, former CIA China mission chief, stated that AI-driven cyber tools would solve the problem of the immense manpower required to scan for and identify infrastructure vulnerabilities likening the process to "a burglar late at night trying front doors one by one until finding an unlocked house." 3. False Data Injection Attacks (FDIA) Academic research has demonstrated that attackers can manipulate power grid measurements and data streams via False Data Injection Attacks (FDIAs), thereby disrupting monitoring and control functions. Targets for such attacks fall into five domains: steady-state control, transient and auxiliary control, substation control, energy and load control, and AI-based systems. 🧨 Tier 2: Physical Attacks Weapons Designed to Cause a "Physical Collapse" of the Grid 1. Graphite Bombs (CBU-94 / BLU-114/B) "Blackout Bombs" These are specialized cluster bombs developed by the United States specifically to target electrical infrastructure. Utilizing a submunition design, the parent bomb releases submunitions upon reaching the target area; these disperse conductive carbon-fiber filaments that cause short circuits and disrupt power supply systems. The weapon saw its first combat use during the 1991 Gulf War, when U.S. forces deployed it via Tomahawk cruise missiles, crippling 85% of Iraq's power grid. During the 1999 Kosovo War, the U.S. military again employed BLU-114/B graphite bombs against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, resulting in power outages across 70% of the country. 2. Electromagnetic Pulse (EMP) Attacks An electromagnetic pulse is a byproduct of a nuclear explosion; if detonated at high altitude, it can cripple an entire power grid system. Experts warn that a single EMP attack would "cripple the already vulnerable U.S. energy grid, wipe out power, and trigger a cascade of deadly events." The United States has been preparing for such attacks for decades. ⚡ Tier 3: Directed-Energy Weapons | A "Long-Range Stranglehold" from the Ionosphere to the Power Grid 1. HAARP: A Geophysical Weapon The U.S. High-Frequency Active Auroral Research Program (HAARP) is capable of precisely beaming high-energy electromagnetic waves with a power output of 1.7 gigawatts (over 70,000 times that of the world's most powerful commercial radio station) at specific locations in the Earth's ionosphere. Russian military experts have noted that HAARP was constructed as a missile defense system designed to manipulate the ionosphere, thereby disabling incoming enemy missiles and aircraft. 2. Directed-Energy "Grid-Kill" Tests Global networks of ionospheric heaters (such as HAARP and EISCAT) and orbital directed-energy platforms possess the capability to induce massive surges of geomagnetically induced currents (GIC) within specific, vulnerable power grids. story-f1e953fb24a3755bd972b7cd.content: Nathan Gabriel Wood’s article, “Explainable AI in the military domain”, is a useful contribution to a debate Ireland needs to take far more seriously: how AI can support defence, security and national resilience without replacing human judgement, accountability or command responsibility. For Ireland, this should not be framed as a conversation about autonomous weapons or removing people from the decision-making process. The more relevant question is how trusted, explainable and auditable AI can support Defence Forces personnel and wider State agencies in areas where we are already stretched: maritime domain awareness, cyber defence, counter-drone detection, logistics, predictive maintenance, intelligence fusion, training simulation and the protection of critical national infrastructure. This links directly to the Commission on the Defence Forces and the move to Level of Ambition 2. LOA 2 identified the need to address serious capability gaps, including improved situational awareness, recognised maritime and air pictures, primary radar, coastal radar, stronger intelligence capacity, cyber defence and a Joint Cyber Defence Command. These are not luxuries. They are basic requirements for a modern sovereign State. It also links to the Defence Forces’ recruitment and retention crisis. AI is not a substitute for fixing pay, conditions, accommodation, career progression or the lived reality of service. Those issues still need to be addressed properly. But used correctly, AI-enabled systems could help reduce pressure on scarce manpower by automating routine analysis, improving logistics, supporting maintenance planning, accelerating information processing and helping small teams manage complex operational environments more effectively. At the same time, AI could create highly specialised roles within the Defence Forces and across the wider Irish defence and security ecosystem. Cyber specialists, data analysts, AI assurance officers, systems integrators, intelligence analysts, digital engineers and human-machine teaming experts should all form part of a modern Defence Forces. These are exactly the kind of high value roles that could help attract and retain technically skilled personnel especially if matched with meaningful career pathways and proper investment. AI will not replace ships, aircraft, radar, communications systems, vehicles, trained personnel or proper funding. However, if developed and governed properly, it can help Ireland make better use of limited resources and strengthen capability in areas where the Defence Forces have been underinvested in for decades. Ireland already has a strong technology sector, a growing cyber ecosystem and world-class research talent. We should be connecting that national capability to defence, security and resilience in a responsible way. That means supporting Irish industry and academia to develop human-led AI tools for maritime surveillance, cyber resilience, secure communications, sensor fusion, emergency response and critical infrastructure protection. Neutrality should not prevent this. A neutral State still needs to understand what is happening in its airspace, waters and cyber networks. A neutral State still needs to protect its infrastructure and people. A neutral State still needs a capable Defence Forces. If Ireland is serious about LOA 2, national resilience, recruitment and retention, and being a leader in AI, then defence must be part of that conversation. AI should not replace our people. It should support them. It should not undermine neutrality. It should make neutrality credible. Neutrality without capability is not strategy. It is dependency. https://t.co/UPCmvDL0al

story-f251c78721430c8633aac13b.content: Export controls assumed AI capability lives in silicon. Reuters just proved it walks out through the API - and once it does, no export control can take it back. On July 31, Reuters and the Jamestown Foundation reviewed 80+ Chinese papers and patents. The finding: PLA-linked researchers are training military AI on outputs from OpenAI and Anthropic models. Not on smuggled chips. On text. The method is model distillation, standard industry practice. You feed prompts to a powerful "teacher" model, then train a smaller "student" model on its outputs, inheriting the reasoning at a fraction of the compute cost. The review documents where it ends up. PLA Unit 96941, the army's main cyber unit, distilled GPT-3.5 to summarize classified source code. Researchers at the North University of China used Claude 3 Haiku to generate synthetic training data for social media monitoring. NUDT distilled a US image model small enough to run on drones for live navigation and targeting analysis. Here is the part Washington should internalize. Export controls are built for physical goods: chips can be counted, seized, sanctioned. A distilled capability is a copy. It runs on domestic silicon, permanently severed from the US supply chain the moment training ends. Anthropic told Reuters it sells no commercial access to Claude in China and warned distilled copies cannot be controlled or monitored. You can gate hardware. You cannot un-copy knowledge. Now the uncomfortable irony. The debate has been framed around open weights leaking capability to China. The review suggests the leak was the closed API all along. Distillation turns a closed frontier model into an effectively open one for anyone with API credits - no weights required. The timing matters. Washington and Beijing are preparing for AI governance talks. The US side frames this as theft, citing watermarks of US models in Chinese outputs. Beijing calls it "AI hegemonism." Both argue over a technique both industries use routinely - US labs distill too, and the frontier was trained on the open internet. The first AI war is being fought with each side's best models as ammunition, and the US models are serving both sides. The next control regime will target the API, not the fab. That fight has already started. #ExportControls #AISecurity #USChina #ChinaAI

At its core was an upgraded version of the Stuxnet virus, designed to specifically infect Iran's energy industry Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems. This system utilizes AI algorithms to efficiently identify software vulnerabilities, map out "vulnerability landscapes," and directly integrate potential targets into US military operational plans. Utilizing a submunition design, the parent bomb releases submunitions upon reaching the target area; these disperse conductive carbon-fiber filaments that cause short circuits and disrupt power supply systems. The weapon saw its first combat use during the 1991 Gulf War, when U.S. forces deployed it via Tomahawk cruise missiles, crippling 85% of Iraq's power grid. During the 1999 Kosovo War, the U.S. military again employed BLU-114/B graphite bombs against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, resulting in power outages across 70% of the country. 2. Electromagnetic Pulse (EMP) Attacks An electromagnetic pulse is a byproduct of a nuclear explosion; if detonated at high altitude, it can cripple an entire power grid system. Experts warn that a single EMP attack would "cripple the already vulnerable U.S. energy grid, wipe out power, and trigger a cascade of deadly events." The United States has been preparing for such attacks for decades. ⚡ Tier 3: Directed-Energy Weapons | A "Long-Range Stranglehold" from the Ionosphere to the Power Grid 1. HAARP: A Geophysical Weapon The U.S. High-Frequency Active Auroral Research Program (HAARP) is capable of precisely beaming high-energy electromagnetic waves with a power output of 1.7 gigawatts (over 70,000 times that of the world's most powerful commercial radio station) at specific locations in the Earth's ionosphere. Russian military experts have noted that HAARP was constructed as a missile defense system designed to manipulate the ionosphere, thereby disabling incoming enemy missiles and aircraft. 2. story-f3cb83be9f34ac9757e58750.content: The Joint Overhead Persistent-Infrared Center brings together military and intelligence professionals to help transform space-based infrared data into timely warning and operational advantage for the nation and the Joint Force. Located at Buckley Space Force Base, Colorado, the JOPC is a joint organization comprising the U.S. Space Force, U.S. Space Command, and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency. Its mission helps integrate Overhead Persistent Infrared capabilities across organizations that depend on those sensors for missile warning, tracking, battlespace awareness, and other critical national security missions. Working within a global network of space command-and-control centers, the JOPC helps synchronize the employment of OPIR capabilities and ensures vital information reaches decision-makers, combatant commanders, allies, and partners when time matters most. Its strength comes from integration—bringing together expertise that crosses service, command, and intelligence-community boundaries to create a more unified picture of threats developing around the world. Military Metal Art is honored to bring the emblem of the JOPC to life. Honoring Sacrifices. Forging Patriotism.

story-f7c1a114a3cdc191b4e1bdf4.content: Officials keep reaching for a Cold War analogy. CIA Director Ratcliffe called advanced AI "akin to digital nuclear weapons." The comparison breaks on contact. Nuclear weapons stayed in state hands and changed little in eighty years. Frontier models are privately built, globally available, and rewritten on a weekly cycle. ⚠️ 🇨🇳 One detail cuts against the panic narrative. US experts estimate China trails by roughly six months on model capability, longer on the chips needed to run them. And unlike missile defense or nuclear arms control, where Beijing won't engage, Chinese officials have reportedly shown more openness to conversations about AI arms control. They may see the capability gap as one area where restraint favors them too. Events shift. Structures move slowly. The Pentagon's Anthropic ban was never really about Anthropic. It was a test of whether the state can regulate a technology it has already made itself dependent on. So far the answer, case by case, has been no. The technology is moving faster than the institutions trying to govern it. That may be the most important national-security problem in the entire NYT piece.

story-f7d8213928f292e232d6e504.content: Then the beginning of the end has arrived. AI gets involved in the war Project Maven is one of the most important AI programs in the U.S. military. It started in 2017 as an effort to use computer vision and machine learning to analyze drone footage and satellite imagery much faster than humans could. Originally, Google was involved, but withdrew in 2018 after internal employee protests. Palantir later became the main technology partner. Today, Maven has evolved into the Maven Smart System — an AI-powered platform that: → Integrates massive amounts of battlefield data → Helps detect and classify objects of military interest → Speeds up the targeting process (the "kill chain") → Supports decision-making across combatant commands It has been reported as a key system used by the U.S. military and is expanding to NATO allies. Palantir remains the primary software integrator. From analyzing drone video to helping prioritize targets at scale, Project Maven represents how AI is moving from experimental to operational in modern warfare.

story-fba744028ed3ca5e7ad3a699.content: "No Consent Required" They didn’t call it a draft, but that’s exactly what it was. In the middle of the Cold War, The United States quietly pulled the highest-scoring children out of normal classrooms and began shaping them for one purpose: national power, technological supremacy, and geopolitical dominance. Selected strictly by test scores, without choice or consent, kids were subjected to specialized education, aka: Their minds were claimed as a government asset. I was one of those kids. No, I am not honored. I am horrified. There is something deeply wrong with a system that decides a six-year-old’s brain is strategic property and then proceeds to “optimize” it under the mask of doing something good for them. In reality, the government walked into schools with the cooperation of the Department of Education, grabbed a select few students, and quietly drafted us. We tell ourselves we need the best human capital in the world. Fine. Competition is real. I'm a big girl now, I get it. But the moment we accept that the state can take children without their consent and feed the essence of their lives into whatever mission it currently has, we have already destroyed something more important than any competitive edge. That same logic is now being applied to the entire planet: We are being forced into a global AI race none of us asked for. This time it's not taking a handful of students into a trailer stationed outside the school for "special classes" then returning them to their "regular" teachers... it's taking the entire population down a path from which there is no return, subjecting them to data centers, massive energy and water use, chips, GPUs, quantum systems, digital ID, autonomous weapons, and a steady normalization of risk, surveillance, and collateral damage. The only question that actually matters is the one the people in charge never seem to ask: What are we losing by winning? Everything else is a prison masked as progress. Progress without consent. --- Thank you for reading. Suzanne Medes, AI Strategist and Technical Writer Just like those "special classes" in my childhood, AI has been put upon us. We are here. How do you make the best of it? Follow me and I'll get you there. I've been taking companies through change before the internet. There are strategic ways to maximize what is being forced upon you and turn it into benefit. I know those ways. Don't Do AI Alone™ FOLLOW ME IF YOU READ. FOLLOW ME IF YOU LOVE AI. story-fbcfff8637382d7879ec335f.content: China is repeating the Soviet Union’s most fatal mistake: trying to compete with a wealthier rival across every expensive frontier at once, and in the process, exhausting itself. The Soviet Union built an extraordinary military machine. Nuclear arsenals. Intercontinental missiles. Advanced fighter jets. Massive warships. Space stations. Moon programs. These achievements impressed the world, but they steadily drained the economy beneath them. The Soviet system poured national resources into projects that generated prestige without creating enough household prosperity, consumer demand, or self-sustaining civilian growth. Eventually, the burden became unbearable. China now appears to be following the same path on an even larger scale. Aircraft carriers are launching at remarkable speed. Naval capacity is expanding rapidly. Beijing is spending heavily on space exploration, artificial intelligence, advanced semiconductors, electric vehicles, biotechnology, nuclear technology, and other strategic industries. Every one of these fields is enormously expensive. And every yuan committed to military expansion, state-directed industrial funds, and prestige technology is a yuan unavailable for household income, pensions, healthcare, education, small businesses, or social security. The consequences are already visible. Chinese consumers remain cautious. Domestic demand is weak. Deflationary pressure persists. Private companies struggle for oxygen. Young people face a brutal employment environment. Factories increasingly depend on exports because Chinese households cannot absorb what the country produces. This creates a dangerous cycle: more subsidies create more capacity, excess capacity creates more exports, and more exports create greater trade conflict. China’s greatest strength would be a wealthy population, a thriving private sector, and a powerful consumer market to reduce the crippling dependence on the US dollar. Instead, Beijing is prioritizing carriers, rockets, factories, and strategic prestige. The Soviet Union already tested this model. The ending was catastrophic. China is heading in the same direction, full-speed.

story-fcb1c3d5fbbba0f65deacec1.content: Battlefield robots open new front in innovation war with major US adversary | Fox News The U.S. Army is teaming up with an artificial intelligence (AI) company to build an AI "brain" for military robots that can think, understand their surroundings and continue missions even after losing contact with human operators as the race for AI dominance intensifies. Working with the Army Research Laboratory, defense AI company EdgeRunner AI has developed an onboard AI system that allows military robots to function in the battlefield without relying on cloud computing or an internet connection in environments where connectivity is lost. "We like to think of robots as the next frontier of AI," EdgeRunner AI founder and CEO Tyler Saltsman told Fox News Digital. "Think of them as a very far-out edge device, kind of like a cell phone, a tablet or a laptop. But now what we can do is we can put a brain, or a neural network, right on that robot so that robots can have context when they're on a mission helping the warfighter." The partnership comes as the U.S. and China race to integrate AI into their militaries, with both countries viewing AI as critical to maintaining a technological edge in future conflicts. Saltsman said it's important for the U.S. to stay ahead in the global AI race, calling China's dominance in drone manufacturing "problematic." "Whether or not China's ahead of us is debatable, but if China is, it's not by much," he said. Saltsman said today's AI is "too generalized," which is why his company is developing technology built for specific military missions. "Warfighters don't need 19th-century poetry," he said. "They need specific intelligence to his or her occupation in order to make better decisions in the heat of battle and that can increase the probability of winning the fight." Working alongside aerial drones, the AI is designed to help robots "problem solve through different routes" while detecting explosives, carrying ammunition, scouting routes and reporting enemy activity. "As you combine them together, you get a much better clarity of the battlefield and increased situational awareness," he said. When communications are cut off, Saltsman said the military will need autonomous systems that can continue making decisions on their own. "You can have a human pilot that controls the ground robot or the drone in the air," he said. "But then if they were to be jammed by a radar jammer and lose connectivity, then the neural network on that robot can still continue the mission and still aid the warfighter." Saltsman argued the military "can't rely on internet access in war," warning that depending on systems like SpaceX's Starlink could add a "risk" to missions. "The problem with Starlink is if you use it, you're effectively showing the enemy where you are, so you might as well be wearing a beacon on you saying, 'Hey, here's where I'm located,'" he said. Pointing to the Russia-Ukraine war, Saltsman said the success of drones has sparked a new push for autonomous ground robots. "As drones have become ubiquitous, now ground robots are like the next thing and then eventually humanoid robots so robots that move and look like humans," he said. Despite the push to advance military AI, Saltsman said safety can't take a back seat and that the technology is built using "transparent" datasets to "understand the biases" of the AI. "That's another thing that differentiates us," he said. "One of the problems is how to use AI safely, how to put guardrails around it and how to understand it." While the technology remains in the "development phase," Saltsman said the breakthrough gives robots the ability to understand what they see, not just detect it. "You can put computer vision models on robots so they can see, but if they don't understand the context of what they're seeing, they're not useful and that's what we're solving for." https://t.co/aX4z8nHx3F

story-fd5d237b5f25c529e4df7d32.content: 🇮🇶|August 12, 2026, Baghdad. Iraqi Prime Minister Zaidi met with U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) Commander Cooper. Zaidi reiterated the September 30 deadline for troop withdrawal. The U.S. is being forced out of Iraq.not because it wants to leave, but because it has no choice. 🎯 The Withdrawal Deadline: A Forced Retreat Zaidi told Cooper that September 30 is the deadline "final and irreversible." On October 1, Iraq will enter a new era free of foreign military presence. Yet, this is not an Iraqi victory; it is a forced U.S. retreat driven by the dual pressures of Iranian missiles and the Iraqi resistance movement. In June 2026, Iranian missiles struck U.S. military facilities at the Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait; satellite imagery showed fires breaking out within the base. On July 29, 2026, the U.S. and Saudi Arabia launched joint airstrikes against Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), killing at least 35 people. In response, the Iraqi resistance issued an ultimatum to the Iraqi government, threatening broader attacks on U.S. interests in Iraq. The U.S. hasn't lost the war but it is losing the occupation. 🩸 The Power of the Resistance Zaidi is not merely conversing with a major power; he is conveying a message from the resistance. The Islamic Resistance in Iraq (IRI) vowed to take matters into its own hands if the government failed to act. The IRI even set a deadline: if the government did not respond to the U.S. airstrikes on the PMF by August 7, they would take action. Zaidi also emphasized "placing all weapons under state control".but in the reality of Iraq, this amounts to demanding that the PMF surrender their arms, even though they are the very force that stood against ISIS and resisted the U.S. occupation. He is attempting to dismantle his own country's defensive capabilities. 💀 The U.S. withdrawal is a tactical adjustment, not a departure The Pentagon is repositioning, not leaving. Defense Secretary Hegseth has proposed redeploying U.S. forces shifting resources from Iraq to Kuwait while bolstering military capabilities remaining in the region. The U.S. is not abandoning the Middle East; it is simply realigning its posture to maintain remote control. The U.S. is withdrawing from Iraq, but it is redeploying elsewhere in the region. It is shifting its military assets from Iraq to Kuwait, Bahrain, and Qatar. It is transitioning from "visible occupation" to "invisible control." When Al-Zaidi met with the CENTCOM commander in Baghdad, he stood at a crossroads. He could order a U.S. withdrawal and face American economic and military pressure, or he could ask them to stay and endure pressure from his own people. Whichever path he chose, the U.S. stranglehold on Iraq would not end, it would merely change form. The empire might withdraw from Iraq, but it will not leave the Middle East. It is simply waiting for a better pretext to return. 🇮🇶
